corrected.name: Common chickweed
corrected.habitat: Cool, moist, fertile disturbed ground — garden beds, lawns, orchard floors, field margins, compost heaps. It's a winter annual that shrugs off frost and keeps photosynthesising near freezing, so in mild Pennsylvania winters it stays green and pickable straight through. Further south and west, midwinter is its peak; it's high summer that shuts it down, since the seed won't germinate much above 86F.
corrected.parts: The whole tender above-ground plant — leaves, stems and flowers. Raw in salads, wilted into soup off the heat, or blitzed into a pesto. Mild and faintly sweet, like corn silk. Cut the mat with scissors and discard the tough lower stems. Eat it as a vegetable, not a staple: the leaves carry saponins, which are poorly absorbed and broken down by cooking, but large raw quantities (a whole-batch pesto in one sitting) can bring on stomach upset. Usually avoided in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

lookalikes.name: Scarlet pimpernel (Lysimachia/Anagallis arvensis)
lookalikes.tell: Square stems in cross-section with no line of hairs — it may carry scattered glandular hairs, but never chickweed's single one-sided line. Leaves stalkless, opposite, often dotted dark or purplish underneath. Flowers salmon-orange, five petals, bluish centre. Chickweed has round stems bearing one narrow line of fine white hairs that switches sides at each node, and white flowers whose five petals are split so deeply they look like ten. Pimpernel contains saponins and cytotoxic cucurbitacins; Oregon State records its folk name as 'poison chickweed' and UC IPM rates its toxicity as ranging from nearly harmless to fatal depending on growing conditions. It has killed livestock and is a real hazard to a child. If the stem is square, do not eat it.
lookalikes.danger_note: Potentially fatal in quantity, especially to children.

lookalikes.name: Petty spurge (Euphorbia peplus) — and other spurges
lookalikes.tell: Snap a stem: every spurge bleeds sticky white latex, while chickweed's sap is clear. That test is the whole ID and it never fails — do it every time. Do not rely on season or sun: petty spurge is the spurge that genuinely grows with chickweed, favouring the same moist, shady flowerbeds, with seedlings emerging from cool autumn weather right through late spring. It stands erect and hairless with oval lower leaves that alternate up the stem and pale green cup-shaped flowers, whereas chickweed sprawls into a mat with strictly paired opposite leaves and that one-sided hair line. The latex causes contact dermatitis, blisters the lips and mouth if eaten, and can do lasting corneal damage if it reaches the eye — don't rub your eyes after weeding. Spotted spurge (E. maculata) is the other common one, but it's a summer plant forming flat mats in hot bare sun, so it overlaps chickweed far less.

lookalikes.name: Mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium fontanum)
lookalikes.tell: Uniformly fuzzy — softly hairy all over both leaves and stems, rather than a single line of hairs running down one side of the stem. Technically edible and harmless, but woolly and unpleasant in the mouth.

corrected.harvest: Shear the mat with scissors an inch above the ground rather than pulling; a single patch regrows repeatedly through the season. It's an abundant non-native annual, so there's no conservation reason to hold back — just don't make it the bulk of a meal. The real caveat is chemical: chickweed thrives on nitrogen-rich ground and concentrates nitrate, sometimes to toxic levels on over-fertile soil, so skip heavily fertilised lawns, manure piles, sprayed beds and anywhere dogs run.

corrected.name: Ostrich fern fiddleheads
corrected.habitat: Stream and river floodplains and damp alluvial bottomland in part shade, under red maple, silver maple and black ash — it wants soil that floods in spring. It grows as a tight circular crown, and last year's stiff, dark-brown, feather-shaped fertile fronds usually stand right in the middle of it. Those standing brown plumes are the surest sign you are in an ostrich fern colony, and they are also the single best way to rule out lady fern, which never produces them.
corrected.parts: Only the tightly coiled crozier, 2–6 inches tall, picked while still tightly curled. Confirm BOTH marks on every fiddlehead, not just one: (1) a broad papery brown scale or sheath wrapping the coil — not fuzz, not wool; and (2) a deep U-shaped groove running down the inside of the smooth stem. Roll the stem between your fingers and you should feel a celery-like channel interrupting an otherwise round stem. Scales alone are not enough — lady fern has those too. Rub the scales off, wash in several changes of water, then BOIL at least 15 minutes or steam 10–12 minutes with a lid, and discard the cooking water. Sautéing, stir-frying and microwaving are explicitly not enough — cook first, then sauté if you want colour.

lookalikes.name: Lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina / A. angustum)
lookalikes.tell: The one lookalike that shares BOTH ostrich fern field marks — the Alaska DNR fiddlehead profile states that lady fern croziers also carry brown papery scales and also show a U-shaped groove, and are hard for an inexperienced gatherer to tell apart. Separate them by the colony, not by the crozier: ostrich fern stands in a tight circular crown ringed by last year's stiff dark-brown fertile plumes; lady fern has only one kind of frond and leaves nothing standing over winter, so a patch with no brown plumes is a patch to walk away from. On the stem itself, lady fern is thinner and light-green to reddish at the base, littered with thin scattered scales that look like hairy legs, versus ostrich fern's broad papery sheath on a stout green stem. Contains thiaminase and must be cooked; if the plumes are absent, do not pick.

lookalikes.name: Bracken fern (Pteridium aquilinum)
lookalikes.tell: The crozier is fuzzy/hairy, has no papery brown scales and no U-shaped groove, and it unfurls as three branching fronds from one stalk. It also favours dry, sandy, open and disturbed ground rather than wet floodplain. It contains ptaquiloside, a proven carcinogen in laboratory animals and a livestock poison. Do not eat it, regardless of what older cookbooks say.

lookalikes.name: Cinnamon fern and interrupted fern (Osmundastrum cinnamomeum, Osmunda claytoniana)
lookalikes.tell: Wrapped head-to-toe in dense tan-white wool that mats and will not brush off; ostrich fern's brown scales are brittle and flake away with a rub. Alaska DNR's rule is simple: if the fiddlehead has fuzz instead of scales, it is neither ostrich fern nor lady fern. Neither has the deep U-shaped groove. Treat as unsafe — these species are the suspected source of some of the fiddleheads behind the 1994 poisoning cases.

lookalikes.name: Sensitive fern (Onoclea sensibilis)
lookalikes.tell: A thinner, smooth stem, often red-tinged at the base, with no papery scales and no deep celery-like channel down the inside — a shallow dip is not the ostrich fern groove. Grows in the same wet ground. Its old fertile stalks are strings of hard dark beads, not the feather-plumes of ostrich fern. Contains thiaminase, is implicated in equine poisoning, and is not considered edible.

corrected.harvest: Pick no more than half the emerged fiddleheads from any one crown, and take no follow-up harvest of later-emerging fiddleheads in the same season — UMaine reports that crowns stripped of all their fiddleheads every year declined and died within four years, while half-harvesting stayed productive. Harvest only from healthy crowns carrying at least four croziers; skip crowns with only one or two. Also treat this as a food-safety plant, not just an ID plant: the 1994 CDC-investigated outbreaks in New York and western Canada came from raw or lightly cooked fiddleheads, with nausea, vomiting, cramps, diarrhoea and headache within 30 minutes to 12 hours. Thorough cooking — boiling 15 minutes or steaming 10–12 minutes, cooking water discarded — is the step public-health guidance credits with preventing it. Never eat them raw, and get landowner permission before picking.

corrected.name: Stinging nettle
corrected.habitat: Rich, damp, disturbed and nitrogen-heavy ground — stream banks, floodplain woods, hedgerows, old barnyards, manure-enriched field edges. It grows in dense colonies, so where there's one there are hundreds.
corrected.indicator: Dense single-species stands on over-fertilised damp ground — old manure piles, barn foundations, silt benches above a creek.
corrected.parts: The top four to six leaves of young shoots under about a foot tall, before flowering. Identify it bare-handed BEFORE you glove up: brush a leaf and stem with the back of one hand. A real nettle burns within seconds, and that sting is the single most reliable field check you have — rubber gloves take it away from you. Then put gloves and long sleeves on and cut with scissors. Never eat raw. Blanching, boiling or steaming destroys the stinging trichomes completely — 1½ to 2 minutes covered is enough, after which it substitutes for spinach in soup, pesto, gnocchi or tea. Native wood nettle (Laportea canadensis), which has alternate rather than opposite leaves and stings just as hard, is picked and cooked identically and is arguably better eating.

lookalikes.name: White snakeroot (Ageratina altissima)
lookalikes.tell: The one that matters — it grows in exactly the same rich damp shade and also has opposite, toothed, pointed leaves. Its white flower clusters are no help: snakeroot doesn't bloom until August–October, so in nettle season both plants are just leafy shoots. Use touch and stem instead. Brush it with bare skin and nothing happens; nettle burns and welts within seconds. Nettle's stem is 4-angled and bristling with stinging hairs, and carries a pair of narrow papery stipules (5–15 mm) at every leaf node; snakeroot is an aster — round green hairless stem, no stipules anywhere, leaves broader and coarsely toothed all round. Do not lean on leaf-stalk length: snakeroot's petioles run up to 2½ inches and nettle's run 1–1½ inches, so they overlap. All parts contain tremetone, the 'milk sickness' toxin; poisoning causes weakness, vomiting, muscle and cardiac damage, and can be fatal.

lookalikes.name: Clearweed and false nettle (Pilea pumila, Boehmeria cylindrica)
lookalikes.tell: No stinging hairs whatsoever; clearweed has translucent, almost watery-looking succulent stems. Harmless, but bland and stringy. If it doesn't sting it isn't nettle — but the reverse is not a safety test, because deadly white snakeroot doesn't sting either. Put any stingless plant back, whichever one you think it is.

lookalikes.name: Horse nettle (Solanum carolinense)
lookalikes.tell: Shares the name and nothing else: it is a nightshade with sharp prickles on stems and leaf midribs, wavy-lobed leaves, star-shaped white or violet flowers with a yellow centre, and yellow tomato-like berries. It grows in open sun, and its prickles jab rather than burn — no stinging-hair welts. Contains solanine.

corrected.harvest: Pinch or cut the tops rather than pulling roots — the plant re-shoots and gives a second cutting from the same stand. The window opens earliest in the maritime Northwest (late February into March) and latest on northern and high-elevation ground (May into June). Nettle is abundant and often weedy, so there's no conservation pressure, but leave plenty standing: it is a larval host for red admiral, question mark and comma butterflies. Stop harvesting once flower tassels appear; older leaves accumulate gritty cystoliths and are conventionally avoided. Skip plants on roadsides or any ground that may have been sprayed.

corrected.name: Dandelion
corrected.habitat: Lawns, pastures, gardens, field margins, sidewalk cracks — anywhere sunny and disturbed. Ubiquitous and non-native, which is exactly why it's the beginner's plant.
corrected.parts: Leaves, crowns, flower petals and roots. Greens are best in February–April (earlier in the South) before the first flower buds open, and again after autumn frosts, when cold sweetens them; blanch or mix with milder greens if the bitterness is too much. Petals go into fritters and jelly; roots dug in early spring or late autumn roast into a coffee substitute. Every broken part bleeds white latex — that latex is the single most useful check in the field, and it can irritate sensitive skin, so rinse your hands after a long picking session.

lookalikes.name: Common groundsel (Senecio vulgaris)
lookalikes.tell: Once it bolts it grows a branched, leafy upright stem carrying clusters of small yellow flower heads with no visible ray petals, sitting in conspicuously black-tipped bracts. But in the February–April greens window it is still a low rosette of deeply lobed leaves that reads as a young dandelion, and none of those flowering marks are there yet — at that stage the test is the sap. Snap a leaf or cut the crown: dandelion bleeds white latex from any break, groundsel's sap is clear and watery. Dandelion also never carries leaves on its flower stalk and never more than one head per hollow, leafless stalk. Groundsel's pyrrolizidine alkaloids are cumulative — small amounts repeated over weeks or months are the real danger, not a single leaf — and the liver injury they cause can be permanent.

lookalikes.name: Coltsfoot (Tussilago farfara)
lookalikes.tell: The trap is the flower, not the leaf, so it matters most when you are picking petals for fritters or jelly. Coltsfoot blooms in March on bare, disturbed ground — roadsides, ditches, gravel, stream banks — with no leaves anywhere on the plant; its hoof-shaped, white-woolly-backed leaves only appear weeks after the flowers have gone. A dandelion flower always rises out of a leafy rosette. The stalk settles it: coltsfoot's is grey-woolly and clad in overlapping scale-like bracts, like a small asparagus spear, while a dandelion scape is smooth, naked and hollow. Coltsfoot's head also has a raised centre disc; dandelion's is all flat strap-shaped rays. Coltsfoot carries hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids, the same class as groundsel.

lookalikes.name: Butterweed / cressleaf groundsel (Packera glabella)
lookalikes.tell: In April it bolts knee- to waist-high on a hollow, deeply ribbed stem streaked reddish-purple, with leaves running all the way up it and many yellow daisy-like heads in a flat-topped cluster — it turns whole Midwest and Southeast fields yellow. Dandelion is a stemless rosette with one head on each hollow leafless stalk. The real trap is earlier: it overwinters as a ragged, deeply lobed rosette sitting right in the March greens window. Break it — butterweed's sap is clear, dandelion's is milky white. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids are present in leaves, stems, flowers and seeds; the liver disease they cause is called seneciosis.

lookalikes.name: Hairy cat's ear (Hypochaeris radicata)
lookalikes.tell: Leaves are covered in coarse bristly hairs and lie flatter to the ground; dandelion leaves are hairless or nearly so. The clincher is the stalk — cat's ear's is solid and wiry, carries small scale-like bracts, and branches to hold more than one head, while dandelion's is hollow (pinch it and it collapses), smooth, naked, and carries exactly one. Cat's ear is edible but tough and hairy, not worth the trouble.

lookalikes.name: Common sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus)
lookalikes.tell: A tall leafy branched stem with clasping, arrow-shaped leaf bases and many flower heads, versus dandelion's stemless basal rosette. Note that sow thistle bleeds milky sap too, so the latex test will not separate these two — go by the stem. Also edible, milder in fact, but not what you think you picked.

corrected.harvest: No sustainability concern at all — take as much as you like; it's a non-native lawn weed and the more you eat the better. The real risk is chemical, not botanical: dandelion grows exactly where herbicides, lawn fertiliser, road salt and dog traffic concentrate. Harvest only from ground you know has not been treated, avoid roadsides entirely, and wash in several changes of water. Avoiding roadsides and ditches does double duty — that is also where coltsfoot and groundsel are thickest.

corrected.name: Garlic mustard
corrected.habitat: Shaded, moist, disturbed ground throughout Pennsylvania — floodplain woods, trail edges, hedgerows, suburban yards and forest understory, where it forms dense carpets that smother spring ephemerals.
corrected.indicator: Wet, disturbed bottomland near creeks and streams. That is also exactly where lesser celandine and poison hemlock grow, so treat a good garlic mustard patch as a reason to look harder at what else is around your boots, not less.
corrected.parts: First-year basal rosette leaves and the slender white taproot in early spring; second-year young tops, flower buds and white flowers before the plant bolts hard. Best flavour is in the first-year rosette; leaves turn sharply bitter once flowering starts. Blanching or a brief boil tames the mustard bite and cuts both the glucosinolates and the cyanide. The root tastes like mild horseradish. One caveat on the smell test, which is the tell that separates this plant from everything toxic near it: the garlic odour is strongest in young spring tissue and gets noticeably weaker with leaf age and after flowering (Michigan State Extension). A strong garlic smell from a freshly crushed leaf is good evidence you have the right plant; a faint or absent smell late in the season is NOT evidence that you do — check the leaf shape too.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.tell: Not a leaf-for-leaf twin — hemlock's leaves are fern-like, three to four times divided into fine lacy segments, while garlic mustard's are simple, kidney- to heart-shaped and scalloped. The danger is that it is the same kind of plant in the same place at the same time: both are biennials of low-lying ground near creeks and streams throughout PA, both are pulled by volunteers in the same weeks, and in May–June both stand three feet or more topped with small white flowers. Hemlock's flowers are flat compound umbels like Queen Anne's lace; garlic mustard's are four-petalled crosses in a narrow spike. Then check the stem: hemlock's is hairless with purple-red blotches (faint at the rosette stage, often merging to solid purple in year two), garlic mustard's is not. Every part of hemlock is deadly and the sap irritates skin — wear gloves when you pull, and never grab a white-flowered top by feel without looking at the leaf it came from.

lookalikes.name: Kidneyleaf buttercup (Ranunculus abortivus)
lookalikes.tell: The closest match there is to a garlic mustard rosette: a native buttercup whose basal leaves are round to kidney-shaped with the same rounded scalloped margins on long stalks, in the same moist bottomland woods, lawns, trail edges and disturbed ground. Scalloped edges do NOT separate the two — the smell does: crush a fresh leaf, garlic mustard reeks of garlic, this smells of nothing. Its later stem leaves are deeply cut into narrow oblong lobes, and its flowers are tiny (about a quarter inch), pale yellow and five-petalled, never white crosses. The sap carries protoanemonin, which blisters skin and burns the mouth and gut.

lookalikes.name: Lesser celandine / fig buttercup (Ficaria verna)
lookalikes.tell: Leaves are glossy, waxy, dark green and kidney-shaped with mostly smooth edges — at most gently lobed or faintly scalloped, never crisply toothed — growing in dense low mats in floodplains, with pea-sized tubers like tiny potatoes at the roots and bulblets on the stems. Crush a leaf and there is no smell. Garlic mustard's rosette leaves are dull, distinctly scallop-toothed and reek of garlic when crushed. Lesser celandine is toxic raw and a Pennsylvania Class B noxious weed — the two grow intermingled in exactly the same PA floodplains in March.

lookalikes.name: Ground ivy / creeping Charlie (Glechoma hederacea)
lookalikes.tell: Square, four-angled stems, kidney-shaped scalloped leaves on long stalks, blue-violet tubular flowers in the leaf axils, and a musky mint smell rather than garlic. It trails and roots at the nodes instead of forming a tidy rosette. Not dangerous to people in the amounts you would eat, but strongly aromatic and bitter — and toxic to horses in quantity.

corrected.harvest: The one plant on this list you should take as much of as you can carry. It is a DCNR-listed invasive that produces hundreds to thousands of seeds per plant — viable in the soil for five to ten years — chemically suppresses native wildflowers and the mycorrhizal fungi trees depend on, and smothers spring ephemerals. Pull the entire root before the seed pods ripen, and bag the plants rather than composting them: flowering plants can still ripen seed after they are pulled. Wear gloves, and look at what you are grabbing — poison hemlock is a biennial of the same wet bottomland and gets pulled in the same weeks. Don't pull the natives by mistake: cutleaf toothwort (Cardamine concatenata) carries the same four-petalled white cross-shaped flowers, but its leaves are deeply cut compound leaves split into narrow fingers, where garlic mustard's are simple and kidney- or heart-shaped. Toothwort is native and slow-growing — leave it be. Two food notes: cyanide in garlic mustard tissue reaches around 100 ppm fresh weight, highest in the youngest leaves of first-year plants — the same rosette leaves that taste best — so chop and cook rather than eating large raw quantities, and start with a small portion if you're sensitive to brassicas.

corrected.name: Ramps (wild leeks)
corrected.habitat: East- and north-facing slopes of rich, moist deciduous forest — near spring seeps, drainages and bottomland that stays damp all season, on calcium-rich soil of slightly acidic pH (roughly 5.5–7.0), often over limestone, in company with sugar maple, trillium, blue cohosh and toothwort. In the southeast this means the Appalachian highlands, not the coastal plain or the Deep South lowlands. Note that deadly false hellebore occupies this same rich upland forest through much of the range, so habitat can never be used to rule it out.
corrected.parts: Usually two broad flat leaves (sometimes one, sometimes three), each rising separately from the ground on its own red-purple sheathed stalk, plus a small white bulb. Leaves raw in salads, grilled, blitzed into butter, compound oils or pesto; bulbs pickled or roasted. Cutting one leaf from a two- or three-leaved plant and leaving the bulb in the ground gives you nearly all the flavour at a small fraction of the ecological cost of digging.

lookalikes.name: False hellebore (Veratrum viride in the north; V. parviflorum in the southern Appalachians; V. woodii in the Midwest)
lookalikes.tell: Leaves are deeply pleated / accordion-ribbed down their length and clasp one stout central stalk, so the plant comes up as a single tight pleated cone from one growing point; crushed, they smell of nothing. Ramp leaves are flat and smooth with no ribbing, each rises separately from the ground on its own red-purple sheathed stalk, and any torn ramp leaf reeks of onion within seconds. DO NOT use habitat to rule this out: only V. viride is reliably a wet-ground plant — V. parviflorum grows in rich deciduous forest at 800–2,030 m through AL, GA, KY, NC, SC, TN, VA and WV, and V. woodii in rich upland Midwestern woods, i.e. the same ground as ramps. Tear and sniff every single plant before it goes in your bag: once you have crushed a few ramps, your hands, knife and bag smell of onion, and a hellebore leaf buried in the bunch will smell of onion too. Steroidal alkaloids bring violent nausea and vomiting 30 minutes to 4 hours after eating, then bradycardia and hypotension; hospital care is the norm and unstable patients need atropine and vasopressors.

lookalikes.name: Lily-of-the-valley (Convallaria majalis)
lookalikes.tell: Paired elliptic leaves sheathing one another at the base and rising from a creeping horizontal rhizome with roots along its length — dig one up and there is no plump onion-like bulb, and a torn leaf has no onion smell at all. Ramps have a single white bulb and reek of onion. Every part contains cardiac glycosides (convallatoxin among dozens); poisoning mimics digitalis toxicity — nausea, slow irregular pulse, low blood pressure, and in severe cases arrhythmia, seizures or coma. Deaths are rare, but hospitalised poisonings from leaves picked alongside wild alliums are well documented in Europe, and NC State's plant toolbox lists it as commonly confused with Allium tricoccum. Do not treat the missing red-purple base as proof on its own: the narrow-leaved ramp (A. burdickii) has pale whitish bases. Smell is the decider.

lookalikes.name: Fly poison / stagger grass (Amianthium muscitoxicum)
lookalikes.tell: Long (15–20 in), narrow, grass- or strap-like basal leaves with a blunt tip and a distinct centre rib, arching out from a bulb that looks convincingly like a small onion — and neither leaf nor bulb smells of onion. Ramp leaves are broad and elliptic (1–3 in across) and the whole plant smells of onion. The real danger is at the bulb: all parts hold neurotoxic alkaloids concentrated in the bulb and NC State Extension states ingestion can be fatal, with salivation, vomiting, weakness and respiratory failure. Native from New York south to Florida and west to Missouri and Oklahoma in moist woods and oak forest, so it overlaps ramps through the southeast and lower Midwest.

lookalikes.name: Trout lily / dogtooth violet (Erythronium americanum)
lookalikes.tell: Leaves are mottled brown-purple and blotchy rather than plain green, are single or paired from a deep corm, and have no onion smell. Not deadly, but strongly emetic in quantity, and it grows in the exact same rich woods alongside ramps.

corrected.harvest: The single most over-harvested spring plant in the East. Rock, Beckage & Gross (2004), working in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, found populations regained pre-harvest density four years after a 10% harvest but not after heavier ones — their sustainable figure is 10% of a patch once per DECADE, not 10% a year. Quebec's assessment is stricter: an annual take of 5–15% of bulbs is enough to send a colony into decline. Nilson et al. (2022, Penn State) found total ramp weight rose 250% and bulb weight 400% between the early 'shoot' stage and the late 'peak leaf/bulb' stage, so waiting about 30 days after emergence — late April into May — and taking the larger three-leaved plants means far fewer plants pulled for the same basket: 'fewer ramps per pound is more ramps in the ground.' Lowest-impact method is to cut one leaf from a two- or three-leaved plant and leave the bulb; this is lower impact, not free — Dion et al. (2016) found leaf harvest can still slow growth by drawing down carbon and nutrient reserves. If you dig, take no more than one plant in ten from a large patch and do not return to that patch for years; never dig a small patch, never dig plants in flower, never dig for sale. Legally: harvesting is banned in Great Smoky Mountains National Park (fines to $5,000), and Quebec has listed ramps as a vulnerable species since 1995 — sale is prohibited and personal harvest capped at 50 bulbs. Check state, provincial and land-manager rules, and get permission before harvesting on any land you do not own.

corrected.name: Common blue violet
corrected.habitat: Lawns and lawn edges, moist woodland floors, stream banks and old fields. It carpets shaded ground alongside other low spring rosettes — harmless ones like garlic mustard, and the genuinely toxic lesser celandine, which is the reason leaf-only identification is a bad habit.
corrected.parts: Leaves and flowers only. Young heart-shaped leaves raw in salad or cooked as a mild, slightly mucilaginous green (useful as a soup thickener); flowers candied, made into jelly, syrup or violet vinegar, or scattered raw over a salad. The leaves contain saponins, so treat them as a salad component or potherb in normal portions rather than a bulk green — large quantities can cause digestive upset. The rhizomes and roots are NOT edible and are emetic in quantity. African violet is an unrelated houseplant and is not food.

lookalikes.name: Lesser celandine / fig buttercup (Ficaria verna)
lookalikes.tell: This is the mistake that matters, because it happens before either plant flowers. Dig and look: celandine has fingernail-sized pale tubers below and small bulblets where the leaves meet the stem, and it runs in dense continuous mats; a violet has a fibrous crown and its leaves rise individually on their own stalks. Leaf surface is the other giveaway — celandine leaves are glossy, waxy and kidney-shaped with mostly smooth or gently scalloped edges, violet leaves are matte and clearly scallop-toothed. In flower it's obvious: celandine has 8 or more narrow shiny yellow petals, violet has 5 irregular purple petals with a spurred lower lip. All parts of lesser celandine are toxic raw (protoanemonin) and the sap can raise a rash or blisters.

lookalikes.name: Wild ginger (Asarum canadense; in the southeast also Hexastylis heartleaf species)
lookalikes.tell: The woodland-floor confusion, not the lawn one — same shaded, moist, stream-bank ground, same spring timing, also heart-shaped. Wild ginger leaves come in PAIRS from the tip of a short stem, are 3–6 inches across, leathery, dull gray-green, conspicuously veined and softly hairy; violet leaves are smaller, thinner, matte green and rise singly and separately from a basal crown. Crush one: wild ginger smells strongly and unmistakably of ginger, violet smells of nothing much. Its flower is a single brownish-purple three-lobed cup sitting on the ground under the leaves, hidden in the litter — nothing like a violet's raised purple flower. Do not eat any part: NC State Extension rates it poisonous in leaves, stems and roots because it contains aristolochic acid, which is nephrotoxic and a carcinogen. The damage is cumulative and silent, so 'I ate some and felt fine' means nothing here.

lookalikes.name: Yellow-flowered violets (e.g. downy yellow violet, Viola pubescens)
lookalikes.tell: Leaves emerge from an upright, hairy flowering stem as well as from the base, and the flowers are yellow with brownish-purple veins on the lowest petal. Genuine violets, not poisonous, but they have a laxative effect — NC State notes the flowers are edible only in limited quantities for that reason. Stick to the stemless blue- and white-flowered kinds, whose leaves and flower stalks all rise straight from the ground.

lookalikes.name: Marsh marigold (Caltha palustris)
lookalikes.tell: Also heart- to kidney-shaped-leaved and spring-flowering, but the scale and the ground are different: glossy leaves 3–6 inches across (larger still after bloom) on thick, smooth, HOLLOW stems, standing in saturated ground, pond edges or shallow water — violets do not grow with their feet in water. Flowers are 1–3 inches across with 5–9 shiny waxy yellow sepals. Contains protoanemonin like the rest of the buttercup family; NC State is explicit that no part of this plant should ever be eaten raw.

corrected.harvest: Identify in flower, always. The single rule that makes this plant safe is the one UMN Extension leads with: every confusable here — lesser celandine, wild ginger, marsh marigold — is confusable only at the leaf stage. Take flowers freely from plants you can see, and take leaves only from a clump you have personally watched produce violet flowers. If you are new to it, take flowers only this year. Beyond that: common and resilient, but not infinite in any one spot — pick flowers sparingly from a given patch and take only a few leaves per plant so the crown keeps producing, and leave enough bloom for the fritillary butterflies whose caterpillars feed exclusively on violets. The bigger caution is where they grow: violets are most abundant in lawns, verges and parks, which are the places most likely to have been sprayed. Harvest only from ground whose treatment history you know.

corrected.name: Wild garlic (field garlic)
corrected.habitat: Lawns, pastures, fencerows, roadside banks, orchard edges and neglected corners across Pennsylvania. A winter perennial: it emerges from the bulb in autumn and does most of its growing while turf is dormant, which is why it shows up from February onward as conspicuous bright green tufts standing proud of a brown late-winter lawn. It persists best where mowing is infrequent, so fencerows, bed edges and pasture margins hold bigger clumps than a closely cut lawn.
corrected.parts: The slender green leaves and the small underground bulb, plus the aerial bulbils that form in a papery-sheathed cluster atop the stalk in late May and June. Use like scallions, garlic chives or garlic - it is considerably stronger than any of them, so use roughly half what a recipe asks. Bulbils pickle beautifully. Treat it as a seasoning, not a vegetable: the sulfides that give it its bite can cause nausea and stomach upset if you eat large quantities raw.

lookalikes.name: Death camas (Toxicoscordion nuttallii and relatives; western T. venenosum)
lookalikes.tell: THE onion-foraging killer in North America. The bulb is oval, brown-coated and looks convincingly like a small onion, but crushed leaves and bulb have NO onion or garlic smell whatsoever - that absence is the entire tell. Leaves are grass-like and V-shaped or keeled in cross-section, never round and hollow like field garlic's, and it grows in glades, prairies, rocky hillsides and unimproved meadows rather than mown turf. Toxins (zygacine, zygadenine) are sodium-channel activators: vomiting, collapsing blood pressure, slowed heart, seizures, death. In 2024 seven members of one family were hospitalised after foraging what they believed were wild onions (Am J Emerg Med, PMID 39472268). T. nuttallii runs from central Kansas and Oklahoma east into southern Missouri, Arkansas and Louisiana - inside the midwest range given here.
lookalikes.sourceNote: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center; Am J Emerg Med 2024 case report

lookalikes.name: Fly poison / crow poison (Amianthium muscitoxicum)
lookalikes.tell: An onion-like bulb topped by grass-like basal leaves, and again NO onion smell when crushed. Leaves are flat, strap-shaped and blunt-tipped with a rounded groove, roughly 1/4 to 3/4 inch wide - never round, hollow and slick. All parts carry alkaloid neurotoxins, most concentrated in the bulb. Grows in open woods, pine barrens, clearings and old fields rather than lawns. Ranges from New York and Pennsylvania south to Florida and west to Missouri and Oklahoma. Note the trap in the name: 'crow poison' is also used for the harmless-looking Nothoscordum below, so never identify anything off a folk name.

lookalikes.name: Star-of-Bethlehem (Ornithogalum umbellatum)
lookalikes.tell: The one most likely to be growing in the same lawn. Leaves are FLAT, not hollow, and carry a distinct white stripe down the midline - and crushing them produces no smell at all. Field garlic leaves are round, hollow and slick, and the whole plant reeks of onion. The bulb looks like a small onion, and the plant is fully leafed out and bulb-only for weeks before it flowers, so through the March-May window you get no flower to help you. This is not merely a stomach upset: the bulbs carry cardiac glycosides - convallatoxin and convalloside (Cornell), rhodexin A and rhodexoside (Purdue) - the same class as foxglove, oleander and lily-of-the-valley, causing arrhythmia and, in sufficient dose, death. Six-petalled white star flowers appear May into June.

lookalikes.name: Daffodil / narcissus foliage and bulbs (Narcissus spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Flat, strap-like, grey-green leaves emerging from the same lawns and beds from March, from an ovoid bulb with brown papery membranes that looks very like an onion - and no onion smell. Contains lycorine and other phenanthridine alkaloids: vomiting, salivation, cramping and diarrhoea, with low blood pressure, tremors and cardiac arrhythmias in large ingestions. This is a real, documented error, not a theoretical one - a published case describes a family poisoned after the father chopped up garden daffodil bulbs instead of onions, and Japan logged 195 accidental daffodil poisonings between 2009 and 2019, one of them fatal.

lookalikes.name: False garlic / crow poison (Nothoscordum bivalve)
lookalikes.tell: The commonest reason a southeastern or midwestern forager gets to use the smell test. It looks like a small wild onion in every respect - onion-like membrane-coated bulb, slender basal leaves, six-parted white flowers - but crushed leaves and bulb have no onion or garlic odour at all. Not documented as deadly, but its toxicity is genuinely poorly characterised, which is reason enough to leave it. If it looks like an onion and smells of nothing, it is not food.

lookalikes.name: Wild onion (Allium canadense)
lookalikes.tell: Not a hazard - a native edible Allium, listed here only so you know which one you brought home. Leaves are flat and solid when cut across, not round and hollow, and it smells properly of onion. Because it is native rather than weedy, harvest it sparingly; A. vineale you can take freely.

corrected.harvest: Non-native and genuinely weedy, so harvest freely - and if you want it gone from a lawn, dig the bulbs, since snapping the leaves only makes it regrow from the offset bulblets. THE RULE FOR THIS WHOLE GENUS: crush a leaf and smell it before anything goes in the basket. If there is no onion or garlic smell, it is not an Allium, no matter how much it looks like one - that single test is what separates you from death camas, fly poison, star-of-Bethlehem and daffodil. But the test has one failure mode you must design around: once you have crushed one Allium, your fingers reek of onion and every plant you crush afterwards will seem to smell of onion too. Test each new plant with clean hands or by tearing a fresh leaf without handling it, and if you are not certain, wash your hands and start again. Back the smell up with the shape: field garlic leaves are round in cross-section, hollow and slick. Nothing on this page's danger list is. Avoid herbicide-treated turf and roadsides, which is exactly where field garlic is most abundant.

corrected.name: Morel
corrected.scientific: Morchella americana, M. angusticeps and allies (Morchella spp.)
corrected.habitat: Rises from bare soil and leaf litter in moist hardwood bottomland and river floodplains, classically around dying elms, ash, sycamore, tulip poplar and old apple orchards; in the West and Northwest the big flushes are on conifer burn sites the first spring or two after a fire. The season tracks soil temperature, so it is a moving wave: the Deep South starts in March, the Midwest and Northeast peak late April into May, and Rocky Mountain burn morels at 8,000-11,000 ft can run through June and into July.
corrected.parts: The whole mushroom, always cooked. Slice each one lengthwise (this both confirms the single hollow chamber and evicts insects), rinse, and cook thoroughly - 10+ minutes of real heat. Never eat morels raw or lightly cooked, and go easy the first time. Even true, correctly identified morels contain small amounts of heat-labile hydrazine-type toxins (Lagrange & Vernoux, Toxins 2020), and the 2023 Montana outbreak (CDC MMWR 73(10)) - 51 ill, three hospitalised, two dead - involved imported CULTIVATED morels served raw and lightly cooked. Right species, clean source, still fatal: cooking is not optional.

lookalikes.name: False morels (Gyromitra spp. - G. esculenta, G. caroliniana in the East, G. montana / G. gigas 'snow false morel' in the West)
lookalikes.tell: The cap is brainlike - irregular lobes, folds and wrinkles that bulge OUTWARD - instead of a honeycomb of pits and ridges that press inward. The decisive test is to slice it top to bottom: a true morel is ONE continuous hollow chamber from cap tip to stem base, while Gyromitra is stuffed with cottony, chambered tissue. Do not treat habitat as a filter: in the West and Northwest, Gyromitra is abundant in montane conifer forest, favours disturbed and recently burned ground, and fruits at snowmelt - the same burn sites and the same window you will be hunting burn morels in. Slice every single mushroom, every time. Gyromitra contains gyromitrin, metabolised to monomethylhydrazine, which is hepatotoxic, nephrotoxic and causes seizures; it has killed people, and cooking does not make it reliably safe.

lookalikes.name: Early morel / wrinkled thimble-cap (Verpa bohemica, V. conica)
lookalikes.tell: Slice it lengthwise - the stem is stuffed with cotton-candy-like wisps of fibre instead of being hollow. That is the test that settles it, because the cap-attachment rule has an exception: half-free morels (Morchella punctipes in the East, M. populiphila in the West) are genuine true morels whose cap is attached about halfway down and hangs free below. Verpa's cap is perched at the very apex of the stem and hangs entirely free like a thimble or skirt, and its surface is wrinkled and ribbed rather than carved into deep pits. Every true morel, half-free included, is hollow; every Verpa is stuffed. Verpa also tends to flush a week or two ahead of the main morel run. It causes GI upset and loss of muscle coordination in some people, sometimes only after repeated meals.

lookalikes.name: Elfin saddles (Helvella spp.)
lookalikes.tell: The cap is a saddle-shaped or irregularly lobed flap, often grey to black, draped over a deeply ribbed and furrowed stem - no pitted honeycomb surface anywhere, and the stem is grooved on the outside rather than smoothly cylindrical. Helvella carry hydrazine-type compounds in the same chemical family as Gyromitra's, metabolised to monomethylhydrazine.

corrected.harvest: Pinch or cut at ground level rather than pulling - yanking rips up the surrounding soil and leaf litter. Carry them in a mesh or basket bag, and resist raking or scuffing the leaf litter, which damages the patch for future years. Leave the tiny ones and any that have gone soft or dark.

corrected.name: Chicken of the Woods
corrected.habitat: Overlapping shelves of bright orange-and-yellow brackets on wounds, stumps, standing trunks and buried roots of hardwoods — oaks above all, also cherry, beech and maple. L. cincinnatus forms a pale-undersided rosette in the soil at the base of oaks. It is a brown-rot pathogen, so the same tree produces year after year. East of the Rockies only: true L. sulphureus does not occur in the West, and the western Laetiporus species are the ones with a poisoning record.
corrected.parts: Only the soft, suede-textured outer inch or two of a young bracket; the inner portion turns chalky and tough with age. Cook it thoroughly — raw or undercooked chicken causes GI distress — and eat a small portion the first time, since some people react to it (upset stomach, swollen lips) even from perfect specimens. Skip fruitbodies on black locust: whether the host matters is unsettled, and locust is argued over often enough that it is not worth the risk when oaks are everywhere.

lookalikes.name: Conifer and western chicken of the woods (Laetiporus conifericola, L. huroniensis, L. gilbertsonii)
lookalikes.tell: Look at the host tree, not the mushroom — the fruitbodies are nearly identical. If it is on any needle-bearing tree (pine, hemlock, spruce, fir, larch/tamarack) leave it: that is L. conifericola or L. huroniensis, repeatedly implicated in vomiting and chills. Treat a yew hedge or shrub as the hardest no of all — yew foliage is cardiotoxic and the mushroom engulfs needles and bark scraps in its folds that survive cleaning. And do not trust 'it's on a hardwood' west of the Rockies: true L. sulphureus does not grow there at all, and the West Coast species L. gilbertsonii fruits on oaks as well as eucalyptus and has a documented record of causing vomiting within an hour, even thoroughly cooked.

lookalikes.name: Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus illudens)
lookalikes.tell: Also bright orange and also clustered at the base of hardwood stumps, but it is a gilled mushroom with a stalk — turn it over and you see sharp, blade-like gills radiating down the stem. Chicken of the woods is a stalkless shelf with a pore surface: a smooth layer of minute holes, never gills.

corrected.harvest: Slice off the tender outer margin with a knife and leave the rest of the bracket attached to the tree — it keeps growing and keeps releasing spores. Take one shelf from a cluster rather than the whole flush, and leave brackets that have faded to chalky white or tan; they are past eating anyway.

corrected.name: Hen of the Woods (Maitake)
corrected.habitat: On the ground at the root flare of mature and aging oaks (occasionally maple, beech or elm) in hardwood forest, parks and old fencerows, mostly east of the Great Plains. In the southeast it is an upland and mountain find: it is very unusual within about 100 miles of the Gulf and is not known from Florida. Peak is mid-September to early October in the north, though it starts in late summer — an August hen overlaps peak season for the black-staining and dyer's polypores below, so run the checks properly that early. A productive tree fruits in the same spot most autumns, so it is worth remembering the oak.
corrected.parts: The tender caps and the fleshy upper part of the branching base; trim off the gritty butt. Never eat it raw — cook it thoroughly, a slow simmer or roast. Try a modest portion the first time: even correctly identified maitake gives a minority of people stomach upset, and true allergy to it exists, though it is rare.

lookalikes.name: Black-staining polypore (Meripilus sumstinei)
lookalikes.tell: Bruises and stains black within minutes wherever it is cut or handled; hen of the woods never blackens. It is also fewer and larger fan-shaped caps (2–8 in. each) rather than dozens of small grey-brown spoons, and it toughens fast and upsets some people's stomachs.

lookalikes.name: Berkeley's polypore (Bondarzewia berkeleyi)
lookalikes.tell: A few very large (3–12 in.) thick, cream-white fans with a coarse pore surface, instead of a rosette of many small grey-brown spoon-shaped caps with a fine white underside. Go by the cream-white colour and the small number of big caps, not by size alone. Young flesh is firm and cuttable, but it turns woody, tough and bitter with age everywhere except the growing edge.

lookalikes.name: Dyer's polypore (Phaeolus schweinitzii)
lookalikes.tell: Grows only on conifers — pine, spruce, larch — at the base or on lateral roots, never on oak. The cap is velvety yellowish-brown to reddish-brown, and critically the pore surface underneath is brownish too; hen of the woods has a white to pale-yellow pore surface on a hardwood host. Inedible, and it fruits early August through September, overlapping the start of hen season.

lookalikes.name: Eastern cauliflower mushroom (Sparassis spathulata, syn. S. herbstii)
lookalikes.tell: Made of flat, wavy, ribbon-like folds with no pore surface at all — run a finger over the underside: the hen has a layer of tiny angular white pores, the cauliflower is smooth. It is whitish-yellow rather than grey-brown. (It is itself an excellent edible, so the risk is not poisoning — but if you cannot tell which one you are holding, you have not confirmed your ID.)

corrected.harvest: Cut the clump cleanly above the base with a knife rather than tearing it out. The fungus lives on as a rot in the roots and lower trunk, so picking the fruiting body does not kill it and the same tree usually refruits for years — just do not dig at or damage the root collar. Take one clump per tree rather than stripping every flush, and grab it while the caps are still firm, because a wet hen sours quickly.

corrected.name: Giant Puffball
corrected.habitat: Open ground rather than deep woods — pastures, meadows, old fields, hedgerows, lawns and woodland edges, singly or in arcs and rings that recur in the same spot, usually a few days after a soaking rain. Peak is late summer into mid autumn; in the lower Midwest and South they can flush as early as May in a wet year (Missouri Dept. of Conservation gives May–October), but Aug–Oct is the reliable window. Mainly east of the Rockies; the western giant puffball is the related Calvatia booniana.
corrected.parts: Only firm flesh that is pure marshmallow-white all the way through. Peel off the outer skin — thin, but tough and hard to digest — then slice into slabs and cook thoroughly. Discard anything yellowing, greenish or powdery inside — the maturing spore mass causes GI upset. Skip lawns and verges likely to have been sprayed, and try a small amount first: some people get a laxative effect even from good specimens.

lookalikes.name: Button or 'egg' stage of Amanita and other gilled mushrooms (destroying angel, Amanita bisporigera; death cap, A. phalloides)
lookalikes.tell: Slice EVERY ball from top to bottom, no exceptions — the test only works on a vertical cut through the middle. An Amanita egg shows the silhouette of a whole tiny mushroom in cross-section: a domed cap, a pale line of gills under it, and a stem running down the centre, all sheathed in a thin membranous universal veil that will become the volva. A real puffball is uniform, featureless white like a marshmallow, with no cap outline, no gill line, no stem. Amanita eggs are also small — an inch to a few inches — so never eat a 'puffball' smaller than a baseball without slicing it, and treat small ones with extra suspicion. Any immature gilled mushroom still inside its universal veil can look like a white ball; the amatoxin species cause liver and kidney failure and are regularly fatal.

lookalikes.name: Pigskin poison puffball / common earthball (Scleroderma citrinum and other Scleroderma spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Judge by the skin and the feel, not by interior colour alone — a very young earthball can still be nearly white inside (MDC: 'When young, the inside is nearly white but soon becomes marbled, then purplish, then blackish with age'). The reliable tells: a thick, tough, rind-like skin, clearly rind-and-core in cross-section rather than uniform flesh; a warty, scaly yellow-brown surface instead of smooth white; a hard, rubbery feel rather than soft marshmallow; and a small maximum size — Scleroderma tops out around 4 inches, while a giant puffball is typically volleyball-sized or larger. Anything marbled, purplish or blackish inside is an earthball for certain. Scleroderma causes severe gastric upset, nausea and vomiting.

lookalikes.name: Stinkhorn eggs (Phallus, Mutinus spp.)
lookalikes.tell: A cut egg shows a distinct gelatinous jelly layer around a dark olive-green core, often with the compressed outline of the future stalk, and the whole thing is soft and often smells foul. Nothing about a giant puffball's interior is layered, slimy or coloured.

corrected.harvest: Cut above the ground and leave the base attachment; take only what you can eat within a day or two, since they turn yellow and inedible fast. Always leave some to reach maturity and release spores — a single giant puffball is a major spore source — and never harvest from sprayed lawns or roadside verges.

unaudited.name: Golden Chanterelle
unaudited.scientific: Cantharellus spp. (C. flavus / C. lateritius in the East, C. formosus in the Pacific Northwest)
unaudited.habitat: Always from soil, moss or leaf litter — never on wood. East of the Rockies they come up singly and scattered under oak and beech through summer after rain; in the Northwest and West the season is a shorter autumn one under Douglas-fir, western hemlock and Sitka spruce in second-growth forest. They are mycorrhizal, so good ground produces year after year.
unaudited.parts: The whole mushroom, cooked. Dry-sauté first to drive off the water they hold, then finish with fat. Chanterelles are not eaten raw.

lookalikes.name: Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus illudens, O. olearius)
lookalikes.tell: It has true gills — thin, sharp-edged, knife-like blades that are crowded, unforked, and can be peeled cleanly off the cap. A chanterelle has false gills: blunt, wax-like forking ridges with crossveins that are part of the flesh and tear rather than peel. Jack-o'-lanterns also grow in big fused clusters from stumps and buried roots, are orange all the way through when sliced, and their gills glow faintly in the dark; chanterelles grow singly from soil and are pale inside. Eating one means days of violent cramps and vomiting.

lookalikes.name: False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca)
lookalikes.tell: Thin, soft and floppy with a brownish-orange, slightly velvety cap and deep-orange, crowded, repeatedly forked TRUE gills. Real chanterelles are thick and firm with a fibrous, string-cheese texture when torn, and blunt ridges. Often on conifer duff or wood chips.

lookalikes.name: Scaly vase chanterelle (Turbinellus floccosus, West/Northwest)
lookalikes.tell: Deeply vase- or trumpet-shaped with coarse orange scales lining the inside of the cup and a pale, wrinkled outer surface. Golden chanterelles are shallowly funnel-shaped and smooth on top. It causes GI upset in many people.

unaudited.harvest: Cut or gently twist at the base and leave the soil intact — never rake or dig the duff, which damages the mycorrhizal network that produced them. Carry them in a mesh bag so spores fall along the way, leave the largest, faded ones to sporulate, and check for state and national-forest permit rules before picking volume in the West.

unaudited.name: Oyster Mushroom
unaudited.habitat: Always on wood — shelving clusters on dead and dying hardwoods, especially fallen aspen, cottonwood, poplar, beech, maple and elm. P. ostreatus flushes in cool weather (late autumn through spring, even after a thaw); P. pulmonarius takes the warm months. Both appear a few days after heavy rain.
unaudited.parts: Caps and the tender part of the short off-centre stem, cooked. Trim the tough base, and check the gills for beetle larvae. Sample a small amount the first time.

lookalikes.name: Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens)
lookalikes.tell: Grows on CONIFER wood — hemlock, fir, spruce — and is thin, floppy, pure chalky white and almost translucent, with essentially no stem. Oysters are thick-fleshed, whitish-tan to grey-brown, and grow on hardwood with a short, stubby off-centre stem. Angel wings caused a cluster of fatal poisonings in Japan, especially in people with pre-existing kidney disease.

lookalikes.name: Deadly galerina / funeral bell (Galerina marginata)
lookalikes.tell: Also grows clustered on rotting logs, but it is a small brown mushroom with a sticky tan-brown cap, a CENTRAL stem carrying a ring (annulus), and a rusty-brown spore print. Oysters have a white to grey-lilac spore print, no ring, and gills running down a stem set off to one side. Galerina contains the same amatoxins as the death cap.

lookalikes.name: Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus illudens)
lookalikes.tell: Bright pumpkin-orange cap, gills and flesh throughout, growing in dense fused clumps from stumps and buried roots. Oysters are white, tan or grey — never orange — and shelve off the side of a log or standing trunk.

lookalikes.name: Bear lentinellus (Lentinellus ursinus)
lookalikes.tell: Gill edges are ragged and saw-toothed rather than smooth, the cap is brown and hairy toward the base, and a tiny taste is searingly bitter and acrid. Oyster gills are smooth-edged and the flesh is mild.

unaudited.harvest: Cut the cluster off at the base with a knife rather than tearing it away — ripping strips the bark and can end the log's production. Leave the small pins and the largest, spore-shedding caps, and don't strip every cluster from one log: a good log will refruit for several years.

unaudited.name: Lion's Mane (Bearded Tooth)
unaudited.habitat: A single white cushion of hanging spines on wounds, broken limbs and scars of living or recently dead hardwoods — especially oak, beech and maple — often several feet up the trunk. Same wound, same tree, most autumns.
unaudited.parts: The whole fruiting body while it is still pure white and firm; slice into slabs and dry-sauté, then finish with butter. Pass on any that has yellowed, which turns sour and bitter. Cook it, and try a small portion first.

lookalikes.name: Northern tooth fungus (Climacodon septentrionalis)
lookalikes.tell: Forms a vertical stack of overlapping shelf-like brackets fused in a row on maple trunks, with short spines only on the underside; it is tough, fibrous and turns grey-brown. Lion's mane is one unbranched cushion with long (½–2 in.) soft spines hanging all over its surface, and no shelf or cap on top.

lookalikes.name: Hedgehog mushroom (Hydnum repandum)
lookalikes.tell: Has a distinct orangish-tan cap on a central stalk with short teeth underneath, growing from soil. Lion's mane has no cap and no stalk, is white, and always grows on wood. (Hedgehog is itself a good edible, but confusing the two means the ID isn't confirmed.)

unaudited.harvest: Cut at the point of attachment and leave the base — the same wound often refruits for several years. Take it while pure white; leave any that have begun to yellow so they can finish shedding spores, and leave some fruitings entirely, as this species is uncommon in many areas.

unaudited.name: Black walnut
unaudited.habitat: Rich bottomland soil, old field edges, fencerows, roadsides and yards throughout the eastern and central US, with open-grown trees bearing the heaviest crops.
unaudited.parts: Kernel only. Hull the green husks as soon as they soften enough to dent under a thumb (late September into October), wash the nuts, then cure them in a single layer somewhere dry and ventilated for two to four weeks before cracking. Wear gloves: the husk juice stains skin, clothing and concrete brown for weeks.

lookalikes.name: Osage orange (Maclura pomifera)
lookalikes.tell: Osage orange fruit is a grapefruit-sized, brain-textured green ball that bleeds sticky white latex when cut; a black walnut fruit is a smooth green sphere 1.5-2 inches across with a single hard brown nut inside.

unaudited.harvest: Collect from the ground, not the tree, and spread your take across several heavy-bearing yard or roadside trees rather than stripping one isolated woodland tree, which is winter mast for squirrels, deer and turkey. Discard any nut that overwintered on the ground or shows mold: moldy black walnut hulls grow Penicillium crustosum, which produces the tremorgenic mycotoxin penitrem A (documented seizures in dogs, and a reported human case).

unaudited.name: Shagbark hickory nut
unaudited.habitat: Upland oak-hickory woods, old fencerows and field edges across the eastern and central US; identify the tree first by the long plates of bark curling away from the trunk at both ends.
unaudited.parts: Kernel, raw or toasted. Gather nuts after they drop; the thick woody husk splits cleanly into four quarter-sections, and if it does not release, dry the nut about a week and try again. Crack with a light hammer tap rather than a lever cracker. No leaching or curing required.

lookalikes.name: Bitternut hickory (Carya cordiformis)
lookalikes.tell: Bitternut has bright sulfur-yellow winter buds and tight, never-shaggy bark, and its husk is thin and leathery, ridged only on the upper half, and will not separate into four free quarters; the kernel is intensely bitter. Shagbark is the hickory with a thick husk that splits fully into four sections.

lookalikes.name: Buckeye / horse chestnut (Aesculus glabra, A. hippocastanum)
lookalikes.tell: Buckeye seeds are smooth, rounded and glossy mahogany with one broad pale scar, shed from a leathery capsule with few or no spines. Hickory nuts are angular and four-ridged, dull tan-white, and come out of a thick woody husk that splits into quarters.

unaudited.harvest: Hickory is heavy mast for squirrels, turkey and bear, so take fallen nuts from several trees rather than clearing under one, and leave the bulk of a poor year's crop. Nuts that rattle, float, or show a small round exit hole are weevil-hollowed and are not worth carrying home.

unaudited.name: Acorns (white oak group)
unaudited.scientific: Quercus alba and relatives (Q. macrocarpa, Q. bicolor, Q. montana, Q. lobata, Q. gambelii)
unaudited.habitat: Oaks occur in every US region — uplands, floodplains, savanna, parks and streets — with the white oak group (rounded, bristle-free leaf lobes) the preferred food group nationwide.
unaudited.parts: Kernel, always after leaching. Shell the nuts, discard any with weevil holes or dark rot, then remove tannins either by steeping whole or halved kernels in repeated changes of cold water over several days to a couple of weeks, or by grinding to meal and rinsing it six to twenty times until it no longer tastes astringent. White-oak-group acorns (acorn matures in a single season, roughly 120 days from pollination) leach in a fraction of the time red-oak-group acorns need. Never eat them raw: the tannin load causes real gastrointestinal upset. Hot-water leaching is fastest but gelatinises the starch, so use hot water for meal you will cook as porridge and cold water for flour you want to bake with.

lookalikes.name: Buckeye / horse chestnut (Aesculus spp.)
lookalikes.tell: An acorn sits in a scaly or bowl-shaped cap and is usually under an inch long. Buckeyes and conkers are 1-2 inches, smooth, round, capless, with a broad pale scar, and drop from a leathery husk rather than a cap. Horse chestnut contains esculin and causes cramping, vomiting and diarrhoea.

unaudited.harvest: Oak mast is boom-and-bust — good white oak crops come only every four to ten years, and in some years there is essentially none — and it is the winter calorie base for deer, bear, turkey and jays. Harvest from the ground in a heavy mast year, take from several trees, and leave poor years alone entirely. Float-test as you go: floaters are weevil-infested.

unaudited.name: Chestnut
unaudited.scientific: Castanea mollissima (Chinese) and hybrids; C. pumila (Allegheny chinquapin)
unaudited.habitat: Realistically found as planted or naturalised Chinese and hybrid trees around old homesteads, orchards, parks and roadsides in the eastern half of the country, plus wild Allegheny chinquapin in southeastern woods and clearings.
unaudited.parts: Nut, roasted or boiled — never raw in quantity. Score the shell before roasting so it does not burst. Fresh chestnuts are starchy rather than oily and spoil quickly; refrigerate or dry them. Note that American chestnut (C. dentata) is functionally gone as a food source: blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) killed roughly four billion trees after 1904, and surviving root sprouts rarely live long enough to bear.

lookalikes.name: Horse chestnut / buckeye (Aesculus hippocastanum, A. glabra)
lookalikes.tell: A true chestnut bur is densely covered in long, fine, needle-sharp spines and holds two to three flattened nuts, each with a pointed tip and a small tassel. Horse chestnut's husk is thick, leathery and green with a few short blunt spikes and holds one large round nut with a broad pale scar and no point. Leaves settle it: chestnut leaves are simple, long and canoe-shaped with hooked teeth; horse chestnut leaves are palmately compound, with five to seven leaflets radiating from a single point.

unaudited.harvest: Most bearing chestnuts in the US are on private or municipal ground, so ask before you gather. Allegheny chinquapin is uncommon and declining across much of its range — take a token handful at most and leave the stand to reseed. Watch for gall wasp and blight; leave nuts from obviously sick trees.

unaudited.name: Burdock root
unaudited.habitat: Naturalised across the US on disturbed, moist, nitrogen-rich ground — barnyards, alleys, vacant lots, roadside ditches, stream banks and pasture edges.
unaudited.parts: The taproot of a FIRST-YEAR plant only, dug in autumn or in very early spring before the stalk bolts; scrub, peel or scrape, and slice thin (it is gobo, the Japanese vegetable). Second-year roots have already fed the flower stalk and are woody and worthless. The young leaf stalks and the peeled inner pith of the young flower stalk are also edible in spring. Burdock is a biennial: year one is a flat rosette of very large heart-shaped leaves, year two a 3-6 ft stalk with the familiar hooked burs. Avoid the mature burs entirely — the pappus bristles cause severe eye, skin and respiratory irritation.

lookalikes.name: Water hemlock (Cicuta maculata)
lookalikes.tell: Not a leaf mimic, but it shares the wet, disturbed ditch-and-streambank ground you dig burdock from, and it is the single reason root foraging is high-risk: a walnut-sized piece of root kills a cow, and death can follow in well under an hour. Its root is a cluster of fleshy tuberous fingers, and a lengthwise slice through the crown shows distinct horizontal chambers and weeps yellowish, oily, mousy-smelling sap. Burdock's root is one solid, unchambered, whitish taproot with no oily sap. Never eat any root you did not dig from a plant you positively identified above ground.

lookalikes.name: Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea)
lookalikes.tell: Foxglove's first-year rosette is the classic burdock mimic where it has naturalised (Northwest, West, Northeast). Foxglove leaves are lance-to-oval with finely toothed margins, dull grey-green and softly downy on BOTH surfaces, and sit over a fine fibrous root that lifts out with a tug. Burdock leaves are broadly heart-shaped with wavy, not toothed, margins, green above and distinctly white-woolly only underneath, on hollow grooved petioles over a thick anchored taproot. Foxglove's cardiac glycosides are not destroyed by drying or cooking, and a fatal case is on record from a similar rosette mix-up with comfrey.

lookalikes.name: Common cocklebur (Xanthium strumarium)
lookalikes.tell: Cocklebur leaves are triangular or maple-shaped and sandpaper-rough on both faces, with no woolly white underside, and its burs are oval with two curved horns at the tip; burdock's burs are round with hooked bracts. Cocklebur seedlings and seeds carry carboxyatractyloside, which has killed livestock and, in famine conditions, people.

unaudited.harvest: Burdock is a non-native weed, so you can dig it hard without conservation concern — just refill your holes and do not spread the burs. The real discipline is safety, not sustainability: roots carry none of the identifying features of the plant they came from, so identify and mark the rosette (or the previous year's dead stalk) while it is intact and dig only what you already identified. Commercial burdock root tea has also caused anticholinergic poisoning from tropane-alkaloid contamination, which is one more argument for digging your own known plant.

unaudited.name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
unaudited.habitat: Native to eastern and central North America and now naturalised in nearly every state, forming dense colonies in moist sunny disturbed ground — roadside ditches, river and stream banks, fence lines and abandoned gardens (ground it shares with water hemlock, so identify by the standing plant, never by the root).
unaudited.parts: Tubers only, dug after the first hard frosts and on through winter whenever the ground is workable. Your identification is the aboveground plant: a 6-10 ft rough-hairy ridged stem, rough sandpapery lance-to-oval toothed leaves (opposite low on the stem, alternate above, on winged petioles), and 2-3.5 inch yellow sunflower heads with 10-20 ray florets. Follow the dead stalk down to the knobbly, ginger-shaped tubers on the rhizomes. Frost converts some of the inulin to sugar and improves the flavour. The tubers store inulin rather than starch, so start with small portions — long slow cooking or fermenting greatly reduces the notorious flatulence.

lookalikes.name: Other perennial sunflowers (Helianthus spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Harmless, just not food: Jerusalem artichoke is the only common tall sunflower that terminates its rhizomes in swollen, knobbly, ginger-like tubers. Annual sunflower (H. annuus) and the woodland sunflowers have fibrous or slender rhizomatous roots with nothing swollen at the end. If you dig and find no tubers, you have the wrong Helianthus, not a hazard.

unaudited.harvest: A colony regenerates entirely from tubers left in the ground, so work the edge of a patch rather than its centre, take roughly a third of what you turn up, replant the small knobs and backfill the holes. Where it is a native stand, do not clear it; where it is an aggressive garden escape or roadside colony, dig freely.

unaudited.name: Sassafras (leaves for filé)
unaudited.habitat: Old fields, woodland edges, fencerows, roadsides and clearings from Maine and Ontario south to Florida and east Texas, spreading by root suckers into clonal thickets.
unaudited.parts: LEAVES, in practice — and this is the honest version of a plant with a bad reputation. Young leaves dried and ground make filé powder, the traditional Cajun and Creole gumbo thickener, and are essentially safrole-free; the FDA permits safrole-free sassafras leaves in food. The ROOT and root bark — the original root beer and sassafras tea material — are a different matter: safrole makes up roughly 80-90% of the essential oil of the root bark, it caused liver tumours in both mice and rats by dietary exposure, the US National Toxicology Program lists it as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen, and the FDA banned safrole, oil of sassafras and safrole-containing sassafras bark as food additives in 1960 (21 CFR 189.180). Commercial root beer has used safrole-free extract ever since. Treat homemade sassafras root tea as a genuine dose- and duration-dependent cancer and liver risk, not folklore. Identification is easy and pleasant: sassafras is the only common native tree carrying three leaf shapes on one branch — unlobed oval, one-thumbed mitten and three-lobed — and a crushed leaf or snapped green twig smells strongly of root beer and lemon.

lookalikes.name: Red and white mulberry (Morus rubra, M. alba)
lookalikes.tell: Mulberry shares the edge-of-field habitat and also produces mitten-shaped and multi-lobed leaves on the same twig, which matters if you are picking leaves in quantity for filé. Crush one: sassafras smells emphatically of root beer and citrus, mulberry has no aroma, bleeds milky sap from the broken petiole and has glossy leaves with sharply toothed margins (sassafras leaf margins are smooth).

unaudited.harvest: Pick young leaves in early summer from suckers and low branches — they regrow, and leaf picking costs the tree almost nothing. Do not dig the roots: beyond the safrole problem, taking the taproot kills the tree, and a sassafras thicket is usually one clonal organism, so digging repeatedly removes the whole colony.

unaudited.name: Elderberry
unaudited.scientific: Sambucus canadensis (American elderberry); S. nigra ssp. caerulea (blue elderberry) in the West
unaudited.habitat: Woody multi-stemmed shrub of stream banks, ditches, wet field edges, roadsides and moist forest openings — American elderberry east of the Rockies, blue elderberry in western canyons, riparian corridors and foothills.
unaudited.parts: Ripe blue-black berries and the white flower heads — but the berries must be COOKED. All parts contain cyanogenic glycosides; NC State states plainly that ingestion can cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and coma, that unripe fruit is far more toxic than ripe, and that cooking inactivates the glycoside. Strip berries off the green stems before cooking (stems, leaves, bark and roots stay toxic no matter what), never eat raw berries by the handful, and skip red-berried species entirely unless you know what you are doing.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.tell: Confusion happens at the FLOWER stage — both carry flat-topped umbrella-like clusters of tiny white flowers on roadsides in early summer. Elderberry is woody and multi-stemmed with opposite, pinnately compound leaves of 5-11 sharply toothed leaflets. Poison hemlock is not woody at all: one smooth, hollow, hairless green stem blotched and streaked purple, fern-like finely divided alternate leaves, and a rank mouse-urine smell when a leaf is crushed. All parts are lethal.

lookalikes.name: Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana)
lookalikes.tell: Pokeweed berries are dark purple-black and grow at the same time in the same waste ground. The plant is entirely herbaceous — snap a stem and it is juicy and hollow with a smooth magenta-to-red skin, never woody. Leaves are simple and alternate, not compound and opposite. Berries hang in one long unbranched raceme like a bead necklace; elderberry berries sit in a flat-topped, repeatedly branching cluster. Berries are the most common route of pokeweed poisoning in children.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa)
lookalikes.tell: Bright scarlet-red fruit in a dome-shaped or conical cluster, not blue-black fruit in a flat-topped cluster. The raw fruit and especially the seeds are strongly emetic and carry higher levels of toxic compounds than blue/black elderberries; if you are not going to cook and strain out the seeds, leave it alone.

lookalikes.name: Devil's walking stick (Aralia spinosa)
lookalikes.tell: Also carries broad clusters of small dark purple berries in late summer. Its trunk and stems are armed with dense sharp prickles and its huge leaves are twice- or thrice-compound; elderberry stems are smooth with raised lenticels and its leaves are once-compound.

unaudited.harvest: Cut whole berry clusters with snips rather than stripping the shrub, and take only a fraction of the clusters from any one plant — elderberry is a heavy late-summer food source for migrating birds. Cutting a few flower heads for cordial removes that year's fruit from the same stem, so choose flowers or berries, not both, on a given shrub.

unaudited.name: Blackberry & black raspberry
unaudited.scientific: Rubus allegheniensis, R. occidentalis, R. armeniacus and other Rubus spp.
unaudited.habitat: Thorny arching canes in old fields, forest edges, powerline cuts, fencerows and clearcuts; the invasive Himalayan blackberry forms enormous thickets across the Northwest and California.
unaudited.parts: Ripe fruit eaten raw or cooked. Black raspberries ripen first (late June-July) and go dull black; blackberries follow (July into September) and are only sweet once they turn from shiny to dull matte black and detach with no pull. Red-stage fruit is just sour, not poisonous.
unaudited.harvest: There are no toxic aggregate-drupelet fruits in North America — every Rubus produces edible fruit — which makes this the safest entry on the list. The practical rule is to watch what else is growing through the thicket (poison ivy, and Virginia creeper's blue-black berries on coral-red stalks, which NC State rates high-severity) so nothing else ends up in the bucket. Canes are biennial: pick the fruit, don't trample or cut this year's green primocanes or you lose next year's crop. Leave the lower and interior fruit for birds and bears.

unaudited.name: Wild blueberry
unaudited.habitat: Acid, sandy or rocky ground — open conifer woods, burned-over barrens, granite balds, old fields and bog margins for lowbush; swamp edges and damp woods for highbush. Maine's commercial wild-blueberry barrens are the classic ground.
unaudited.parts: Ripe fruit raw, cooked or frozen. Blue-black with a powdery bloom; genuinely ripe berries fall into your hand.

lookalikes.name: Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) / glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus)
lookalikes.tell: The decisive test is the blossom end: a true blueberry carries a persistent five-pointed calyx — a little star-shaped crown — opposite the stem. Buckthorn's glossy black drupe has no crown, holds 3-4 hard seeds, and grows on a shrub or small tree whose twigs end in a short straight thorn and whose leaves have veins curving forward toward the tip. It also ripens later, August-September, and its fruit contains glycosides that cause nausea, vomiting and violent diarrhea.

lookalikes.name: Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana)
lookalikes.tell: Purple-black and glossy, but borne in a long unbranched drooping raceme on a soft magenta-stemmed herb up to 9 feet tall, not on a low twiggy woody shrub. Each berry is slightly flattened with a plain flat scar at the tip — no five-pointed crown. Berries are the usual cause of pokeweed poisoning in children.

unaudited.harvest: Hand-pick rather than raking or stripping twigs — pulling leaves and stems off wild plants damages the rhizomes that lowbush blueberry regenerates from. Leave a good share: barrens berries are a major late-summer food for bears and birds. Check rules before picking in national/state parks and on tribal or commercially managed barrens.

unaudited.name: Pawpaw
unaudited.habitat: Clonal understory patches in rich, moist bottomland forest and shady river and creek terraces; native to 26 states from northern Florida to southern Ontario and west to eastern Nebraska. Large drooping leaves and a tropical look give the patch away long before the fruit does.
unaudited.parts: Ripe pulp only, raw or in custards and ice cream — banana-mango-custard flavour. Ripe fruit yields to a gentle tug and gives softly under the thumb. Do NOT eat the skin or the big brown seeds: NC State attributes stomach and intestinal pain to eating skin or seeds, notes the acetogenins in the plant, and lists contact dermatitis from handling fruit. A minority of people get a GI or allergic reaction to the pulp itself, so try a small amount the first time.
unaudited.harvest: Never pull unripe fruit — it will not ripen properly and you have wasted it. Pick only fruit that releases with a light tug, or shake the small tree and take what drops. Patches are clonal and self-incompatible, so fruit set is often poor; take a share and leave the rest, and don't cut or break branches to reach clusters.
