unaudited.name: Serviceberry (juneberry, saskatoon)
unaudited.scientific: Amelanchier spp. (A. arborea, A. laevis, A. canadensis, A. alnifolia)
unaudited.habitat: Small trees and shrubs of forest edges, fencerows, roadsides, cliffs and balds, plus heavily planted as a street and yard tree; A. alnifolia (saskatoon) fills the same role in the Northwest and Rockies and A. utahensis in the Great Basin.
unaudited.parts: Ripe fruit raw or cooked — a berry-like pome the size of a blueberry that ripens through red to deep purple-black, sweet with an almond note from the soft seeds. Cook and run through a food mill if the seeds bother you.

lookalikes.name: Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica)
lookalikes.tell: Similar-sized glossy black fruit in similar hedgerow habitat. Timing is the first filter: serviceberry ripens in May-June, buckthorn not until August-September. Then look at the fruit tip — serviceberry keeps a five-lobed calyx crown at the blossom end like a tiny apple, buckthorn does not, and buckthorn fruit splits to reveal 3-4 hard seeds. Buckthorn twigs end in a short thorn and its leaf veins curve forward toward the tip.

lookalikes.name: Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana)
lookalikes.tell: Also dark and shrubby, but chokecherry fruit hangs in long cylindrical racemes and each fruit has one hard stone; serviceberry fruit sits in short loose clusters and is soft with several small seeds. Chokecherry flesh is edible but mouth-puckeringly astringent raw, and its stones, leaves and twigs are cyanogenic — never crush the pits.

unaudited.harvest: Birds strip a tree in days, so competition is real — take part of a tree, not all of it. Pick from the outside and don't break or bend branches; serviceberry keeps ripening after picking, so slightly under-ripe fruit is fine to gather.

unaudited.name: Mulberry
unaudited.scientific: Morus rubra (red mulberry); Morus alba (white mulberry, naturalized)
unaudited.habitat: Red mulberry in rich woods and bottomlands of the eastern US; white mulberry naturalized nearly everywhere in old fields, urban lots, alleys, roadsides and forest edges, including throughout the West and Great Plains where it was planted by the million for windbreaks.
unaudited.parts: Fully ripe fruit only, raw or in pies, jams and syrups. Ripe means deep purple-black (or, on white-fruited trees, soft and translucent) and dropping at a touch. Unripe fruit and the milky white sap that runs from every part of the tree cause stomach upset and, per NC State, hallucinations; the sap can also cause contact dermatitis. Ripe fruit is harmless.
unaudited.harvest: Spread a sheet or tarp under the tree and shake — this is far easier than picking and takes only what is truly ripe. Mulberry (especially naturalized white mulberry, a listed invasive in Wisconsin, Indiana and Ohio) fruits so heavily that over-harvest is not a concern; the fruit is a major bird food, and the tree drops far more than anyone can gather.

unaudited.name: American persimmon
unaudited.habitat: Old fields, fencerows, roadsides, woodland edges and poor dry uplands from New England south to Florida and west to Texas and Kansas; fruit often hangs on bare branches after the leaves drop, which is when it is easiest to spot.
unaudited.parts: Only fully ripe fruit — squishy-soft, deep orange, wrinkling, and usually already on the ground. Unripe persimmon is loaded with tannins and is fiercely astringent; eating a lot of unripe fruit is the documented cause of diospyrobezoars, hard tannin masses that can obstruct the stomach or bowel. Astringency goes with ripeness, not with cold: Purdue Extension states outright that the fruit does not have to experience a frost to ripen. Frost simply happens to arrive around the same time. Skin, cook, or pass the pulp through a food mill to remove the large flat seeds.
unaudited.harvest: Gather windfalls — shaking or picking firm fruit off the tree just gets you astringent fruit and wastes it. Persimmon is a heavy autumn food for deer, foxes, raccoons and opossums, so clear only part of the drop under any one tree and come back on later visits rather than stripping it once.

unaudited.name: Beach plum
unaudited.habitat: Low sprawling shrub of Atlantic coastal sand — foredunes, back-dune scrub and sandy coastal plain from New Brunswick and Maine south to Maryland and Virginia; abundant on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and the Jersey Shore, and widely planted for dune stabilisation.
unaudited.parts: Ripe fruit, almost always cooked into jam, jelly or syrup — it is high in pectin and tart. Fruit is under an inch across and ripens purple, blue-black or occasionally yellow from late August through early October, peaking in September. As with all Prunus, the stones, leaves and twigs are cyanogenic: eat the flesh, never crush or eat the pits.

lookalikes.name: American plum (Prunus americana), Canada plum (P. nigra), black cherry (P. serotina)
lookalikes.tell: Genuinely confusable relatives, but all have edible flesh, so a mix-up is disappointing rather than dangerous. Beach plum is the only one that is a low, sprawling, often knee-to-shoulder-high shrub growing directly in loose coastal sand; the others are upright shrubs or trees of inland thickets and woods. Black cherry fruit is small, black and borne in long racemes, not single or paired on short stalks. In every case the stone stays uneaten.

lookalikes.name: Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana)
lookalikes.tell: Fruit hangs in long cylindrical clusters rather than singly or in twos along the twig, and the flesh is harshly astringent raw. Edible cooked, but not what you came for.

unaudited.harvest: Dunes are the fragile part, not the plant. Stay on established paths and off the dune face — trampling does more damage than picking. Beach plum is state-listed as endangered in Maine (S1) and its habitat has been squeezed hard by beachfront development, so in the northern part of the range take nothing. Many town beaches, state parks and National Seashore areas restrict or prohibit picking; check first, then take a modest share and leave fruit on each bush.

unaudited.name: Glasswort / Sea Beans
unaudited.scientific: Salicornia spp. (S. depressa, S. bigelovii on the Atlantic; S. pacifica, formerly Sarcocornia pacifica, on the Pacific)
unaudited.habitat: Coastal salt marshes, tidal mudflats and the brackish margins of beaches and estuaries, where it is often the pioneer plant colonizing bare mud; also inland alkaline seeps and salt flats in the West.
unaudited.parts: Only the tender upper stem tips, taken where they snap off cleanly. Eaten raw in salads, blanched, quickly sauteed, or pickled. Already intensely salty, so cook with no added salt; older lower stems turn woody and stringy and are not worth taking.

lookalikes.name: Seaside arrowgrass (Triglochin maritima)
lookalikes.tell: Arrowgrass grows in the same salt marshes but its leaves are narrow, half-round, grass-like blades rising in a basal tuft from a papery sheath, and its green leaves contain the cyanogenic glycosides triglochinin and taxiphyllin, which release hydrogen cyanide when chewed or crushed. Salicornia has no leaves at all — just obviously jointed, segmented leafless succulent stems like strings of tiny pickles.

unaudited.harvest: Pinch the top few inches and leave the plant rooted — Salicornia stabilizes bare marsh mud and regrows from what you leave. Never pull it up. Skip marshes below storm drains, marinas or industrial sites; halophytes concentrate whatever is in the sediment. On the Pacific coast much pickleweed marsh is protected habitat for the endangered salt marsh harvest mouse and Ridgway's rail — check ownership and rules before cutting anything.

unaudited.name: Bull Kelp (Bullwhip Kelp)
unaudited.habitat: Rocky subtidal reefs and channels with cold, moving water from central California north through Alaska. An annual: a long hollow stipe rises from a rock holdfast to a single gas-filled bulb at the surface with long blades trailing on the tide — reachable at low tide from rocks or by kayak.
unaudited.parts: Blades for salads, stir-fries, soups, or dried as a seasoning; the hollow stipe and bulb are most often pickled. Rinse off the salt and peel away the tough brown outer layer to reach the pale green flesh.

lookalikes.name: Acid kelp / witch's hair (Desmarestia spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Desmarestia is finely branched and feathery with no hollow stipe and no float bulb, and it stores sulfuric acid in its cells at a pH as low as 0.5 — it tastes acrid, and if bruised it will discolor and rot every other seaweed sharing your bag. Bull kelp is unmistakable: one long hollow whip ending in a single round float.

unaudited.harvest: Cut blades with a knife at least 24 inches above the bulb and never tear the plant loose or disturb the holdfast — Washington codifies this, requires a Shellfish/Seaweed or combination license, and caps personal harvest at 10 lb wet weight per person per day, with most state parks and marine preserves closed. Kelp forests are declining habitat; take a few blades from several plants rather than stripping one, and stay well away from harbors and outfalls.

unaudited.name: Staghorn Sumac
unaudited.habitat: Dry, sunny, well-drained ground — roadside banks, railroad embankments, old fields and woodland edges — spreading into dense clonal thickets from Quebec and Ontario south to Georgia and west to Minnesota and Iowa. It does not grow in standing water.
unaudited.parts: The dense red drupe clusters ("bobs"), taken when deep rust-red. Bruise whole cones and steep them in COLD water for several hours, then strain through cloth for tart pink sumac-ade — hot water pulls bitter tannin out of the seeds and stems. Dried and rubbed off the stem, the drupes grind into the tart red spice used in za'atar. Fruit forms on female plants only.

lookalikes.name: Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix)
lookalikes.tell: Poison sumac grows exclusively in standing water — swamps, bogs, fens, wooded wetlands — as scattered single plants, has 7–13 smooth-edged, hairless leaflets on a reddish central leaf stalk, and carries whitish-green berries in loose clusters that HANG DOWN. Staghorn has 11–31 saw-toothed leaflets, velvety reddish-brown fuzz on its young twigs, dense red cones held UPRIGHT above the leaves, and forms colonies on dry ground. Poison sumac carries the same urushiol as poison ivy and the reaction is worse.

unaudited.harvest: Pick whole cones after several dry days and before rain — the tart coating is water-soluble and rain rinses it away. Cut a few cones per clone and leave the rest; the fruit is important late-winter food for robins, bluebirds and grouse. Skip roadside plants likely to have been sprayed or road-salted.

unaudited.name: Spicebush
unaudited.habitat: Understory shrub of moist, rich deciduous woods across the eastern US — bottomlands, stream banks, wooded swamps and pond shores, occasionally on drier uplands.
unaudited.parts: Ripe scarlet, football-shaped berries (female plants only), dried and ground into an allspice-meets-citrus-pepper spice. Twigs and leaves make a warm tea and can be cut year-round. The flavor is strong — use a light hand.

lookalikes.name: Asian bush honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii, L. morrowii, L. tatarica)
lookalikes.tell: Honeysuckle leaves and berries are OPPOSITE and paired; the translucent red berries sit in twos with a dark dimple at the base, the older stems are hollow, and nothing about the plant smells of spice. Spicebush leaves and berries are alternate, and a scratched twig smells intensely of cloves, anise and citrus. Honeysuckle berries contain saponins and cause abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea.

lookalikes.name: Winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata)
lookalikes.tell: Winterberry leaves have clearly toothed margins and no aroma at all when crushed, and its round red berries cling to bare branches deep into winter. Spicebush leaves are entire (untoothed) and powerfully aromatic, and its oval berries are stripped by birds by late October. Winterberry fruit causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.

lookalikes.name: Carolina and common buckthorn (Frangula caroliniana, Rhamnus cathartica)
lookalikes.tell: Buckthorn leaves have strongly arcuate veins that sweep forward toward the leaf tip and are odorless when crushed; the fruit ripens through red to black and acts as a violent laxative. Spicebush veins are not conspicuously curved and the crushed leaf is unmistakably spicy-citrus.

unaudited.harvest: Scratch a twig and smell it before you pick anything — that is the whole test, and no lookalike passes it. Only female shrubs fruit and birds strip them within days of ripening, so take a modest handful and move on. Cut twigs sparingly across several shrubs rather than stripping one; spicebush is the host plant for the spicebush swallowtail.

unaudited.name: Wild Bergamot / Bee Balm
unaudited.habitat: Dry to moderately moist open ground across most of North America — tallgrass prairie, glade and rocky woodland margins, unplanted fields, fencerows and roadsides in full sun.
unaudited.parts: Leaves and the shaggy lavender-pink flower heads, fresh or dried. Carvacrol and thymol give it an oregano-and-thyme flavor: good in bean and tomato dishes, meat rubs, and steeped as tea. Roots are not used. Confirm three things before picking — a square, hollow stem, opposite toothed grayish-green leaves, and a strong oregano smell from a crushed leaf.

lookalikes.name: Spotted horsemint (Monarda punctata)
lookalikes.tell: Same genus, same square stem and aromatic leaf, but its flowers are pale yellow blotched with purple, stacked in whorls above showy pink-and-white bracts down the stem. Its thymol content is high enough to taste harsh and medicinal rather than pleasant. Wild bergamot carries a single shaggy lavender-pink pompom at the top of the stem.

unaudited.harvest: Cut the top third of flowering stems with scissors and leave the rest standing. Wild bergamot is a first-rank nectar plant for bees, hummingbirds and butterflies, and native bees nest inside the hollow dead stems over winter — so leave dead stems up. Take from large stands only, never more than a small fraction, and leave plenty of flowers to set seed.

unaudited.name: Prickly Pear
unaudited.scientific: Opuntia spp. (O. engelmannii, O. ficus-indica in the Southwest; O. humifusa in the East)
unaudited.habitat: Dry, sunny, sharply drained ground — desert flats and bajadas in the Southwest; sand dunes, shale barrens, pine barrens and coastal sand in the East, where O. humifusa reaches New England and eastern Pennsylvania.
unaudited.parts: Young spring pads (nopales) grilled, griddled or diced, and ripe late-summer fruit (tunas) for juice, syrup and jelly. Pads are best picked mid-morning to mid-afternoon when acid content is lowest. Fruit does not ripen after picking — take it deep red-purple and yielding.

lookalikes.name: Cholla (Cylindropuntia spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Cholla stems are cylindrical, jointed rods rather than flat paddles, its spines wear loose papery sheaths, and whole barbed segments detach and stick to skin and clothing far more stubbornly than prickly pear glochids. Its fruit is dry and spiny, not the juicy tuna. Prickly pear is always a flat, paddle-shaped pad.

unaudited.harvest: Glochids are the real hazard here, not misidentification. The hair-fine barbed bristles clustered at the base of the big spines detach on contact and lodge in skin, lips and eyes, and even "spineless" varieties have them. Wear leather gloves, use tongs and a long knife, and burn or scrape the glochids off BEFORE any rinsing — water just spreads them. Cut pads cleanly at the joint, take only one or two per plant, and leave fruit for wildlife in dry years. Arizona's Native Plant Law protects native cacti from removal or mutilation, and collecting anywhere requires the landowner's permission.

unaudited.name: Common Juniper
unaudited.habitat: Dry, open, rocky hillsides, sand terraces, maritime escarpments and exposed slopes, usually as a low sprawling mat rather than a tree. Circumboreal: Alaska and British Columbia east to Newfoundland, south through New England to the Carolina mountains and through the western mountains to California, Arizona and New Mexico.
unaudited.parts: Only the ripe, waxy blue-black second- or third-year cones ("berries"). Dry and crush them for a resinous, gin-like spice — game, cured pork, brines, sauerkraut, braised cabbage. Use a few berries, not a spoonful: juniper is a gastrointestinal and kidney irritant in quantity, and is avoided in pregnancy and by anyone with kidney disease.

lookalikes.name: Yew (Taxus canadensis in the wild; T. cuspidata and T. x media in hedges)
lookalikes.tell: Yew is the one that kills. Its needles are flat, soft and set in two flat ranks along either side of the twig, dark above and pale beneath, and its fruit is a bright red, fleshy, OPEN-ENDED cup with a single dark seed visible at the tip. Common juniper's needles are stiff and sharp-tipped, set in whorls of THREE around the twig, each with one broad white stripe on the upper surface, and its fruit is a hard, closed, waxy blue-black cone. Yew seeds and foliage contain taxine, a rapidly absorbed cardiac depressant that can kill within hours.

lookalikes.name: Savin juniper (Juniperus sabina)
lookalikes.tell: Savin is a widely planted ground-cover juniper whose mature foliage is scale-like and overlapping, pressed flat against the twig, with a rank, acrid smell when crushed. Common juniper never develops scale leaves — it keeps sharp needles in whorls of three for its entire life. Savin contains sabinyl acetate, sabinol and podophyllotoxin; ingestion causes necrosis of the kidneys, and its historical use as an abortifacient was frequently fatal.

unaudited.harvest: Verify the whorls-of-three sharp needles and the single broad white stripe on every plant before you pick, and never forage "juniper" out of ornamental plantings — savin and yew are both common landscape shrubs. Common juniper is slow-growing and individual plants live over 170 years; take a small handful of ripe cones from a large stand and leave the rest for the birds that disperse them.

unaudited.name: Bayberry / Wax Myrtle
unaudited.scientific: Morella pensylvanica (syn. Myrica pensylvanica), northern bayberry; Morella cerifera (syn. Myrica cerifera), southern wax myrtle
unaudited.habitat: Coastal sand dunes, back-dune thickets, pine barrens, forest edges and the upland margins of tidal marshes — northern bayberry along the northeastern coast south to North Carolina, wax myrtle through the Southeast. Both are strongly tolerant of salt spray and saline soil.
unaudited.parts: The leaves, used exactly like a bay leaf — dried and simmered whole in stocks, beans, braises and pickling brines, then fished out before serving. Northern bayberry is milder than Mediterranean bay, so use roughly twice as many leaves; drying concentrates the aroma. Harvest leaves any time they are green and pliable. The gray waxy fruit is candle and soap material, not food — there is almost no flesh on it. Do not use the root bark; that is a medicinal preparation, not a kitchen ingredient.

lookalikes.name: Groundsel tree / eastern baccharis (Baccharis halimifolia)
lookalikes.tell: Baccharis shares exactly the same dune edges and marsh-border thickets, but its wedge-shaped, coarsely toothed gray-green leaves have NO smell when crushed, and in autumn it is covered in conspicuous fluffy white seed heads. Its leaves and flowers contain a cardioactive glycoside. Bayberry and wax myrtle leaves are untoothed or only bluntly toothed toward the tip, speckled with yellow resin dots on the underside, and rubbing one releases the unmistakable bayberry-candle scent.

unaudited.harvest: Rub and smell a leaf every single time — the resinous bayberry-candle aroma is the identification. Strip a few leaves from several branches rather than defoliating one stem; these are slow-growing dune stabilizers, and the waxy fruit is critical winter food for yellow-rumped warblers, one of the few birds able to digest the wax. The plants are dioecious, so leave fruiting (female) shrubs alone and take leaves from males where you can tell them apart.

audit_problems.name: Common chickweed
problems: WRONG SPURGE NAMED, AND ITS TELL IS ACTIVELY MISLEADING (main safety defect). The entry headlines spotted spurge (Euphorbia maculata), which UC IPM and MSU confirm is a STRICTLY SUMMER annual forming prostrate mats on 'harsh full-sun baked sites' — a species that barely co-occurs with cool-season chickweed. The spurge foragers actually confuse with chickweed is petty spurge (Euphorbia peplus): UC IPM describes it in gardens that are 'moist and shady... among shrubs and flowerbeds,' and NC State says its seedlings emerge 'beginning in the cool weather of fall and continue through late spring' — chickweed's exact niche and exact season. The entry's tell 'spurge also sprawls flat in hot dry sun where chickweed won't grow' is therefore FALSE for the spurge you would really meet, and fails in the one scenario that matters: it would falsely reassure someone that the erect plant in their shady March bed cannot be spurge. NC State rates E. peplus sap as capable of causing 'temporary to permanent corneal damage' and blistering of lips and mouth. Fixed: petty spurge is now the headline, the latex test leads, the false sun/season tell is removed and replaced with erect-and-hairless vs sprawling-mat-with-hair-line.

MONTHS CONTRADICT THE ENTRY'S OWN HABITAT TEXT. months [2,3,4,9,10] = Mar-May + Oct-Nov, excluding Dec/Jan/Feb — yet the habitat field states it 'stays green and pickable straight through' mild Pennsylvania winters. UC IPM confirms seeds germinate 'January through early March,' advises monitoring 'throughout late fall and winter,' and sources note it grows most aggressively in late winter/early spring; it photosynthesizes below 5C. With regions:['all'], midwinter is PEAK chickweed in the west and southeast (Clemson and UC IPM both treat it as a winter annual). Fixed to [0,1,2,3,4,9,10,11] — everything except true summer heat (SARE: will not germinate above 86F).

SAPONIN MODERATION CAVEAT MISSING. The caution covers only nitrates. NC State notes the leaves contain saponins ('toxic... but very poorly absorbed,' 'broken down by thorough cooking') and PFAF/Herbal Reality advise against eating large quantities RAW, citing diarrhoea/vomiting, and against use in pregnancy or breastfeeding. This matters here specifically because the entry recommends blitzing it into pesto — a large raw dose — and tells the reader to 'take freely.' Added a moderation line to parts and harvest.

SCARLET PIMPERNEL DANGER ARGUABLY UNDERSTATED — considered and deliberately left at 'toxic'. UC IPM states its toxicity 'ranges from virtually nontoxic to fatally toxic,' and foraging sources note it 'can be deadly,' most plausibly in children. I did NOT promote it to 'deadly' or push overall caution to 'expert': there are no documented human fatalities, UC IPM's fatal range refers to grazing livestock, and the separation tells are unusually robust (square hairless stem vs round stem with a one-sided hair line; orange vs white flowers). Calling chickweed an expert-tier forage would be miscalibrated against genuine expert cases like ramps/lily-of-the-valley. Instead the tell now states the fatality potential explicitly and adds OSU's documented alias 'poison chickweed' so the reader is not under-informed.

NO SOURCE FOR TWO OF THREE LOOKALIKES. Three citations supported scarlet pimpernel; zero supported the spurge or mouse-ear claims. Added UC IPM and NC State petty spurge pages (both verified real) plus the UC IPM Chickweeds page to support the corrected seasonality.

PIMPERNEL HAIR CLAIM SLIGHTLY IMPRECISE. Entry said 'no hair line at all'; UC IPM actually contrasts 'the square stems and glandular hairs of scarlet pimpernel' with chickweed's 'round stems and nonglandular hairs' — so pimpernel does bear scattered glandular hairs, it just lacks the one-sided line. Reworded to say so precisely, since a forager who finds any hair at all on a square stem should not be talked out of the ID.

VERIFIED SOUND, NO CHANGE NEEDED: All six original sources are real and authoritative — no fabricated citations. Cornell CALS, NC State, UC IPM, OSU and SARE resolved directly; the Virginia Tech profile/797 URL returned 403 to the fetcher but was confirmed genuine via search. Regions 'all' is correct (VT: 'distributed throughout the United States'; NC State: cosmopolitan, naturalized across North America). No DEADLY lookalike is missing — scarlet pimpernel and spurge are the two canonical poisonous confusables in the literature and both were present. The pimpernel tells (square stem, sessile leaves with dark/purplish glands beneath, salmon-orange flowers with bluish centre, saponins and cucurbitacins) are corroborated near-verbatim by UC IPM and OSU. The deeply-notched 5-petals-look-like-10 tell, the corn-silk flavour note, the mouse-ear 'uniformly fuzzy / unpalatable' rating, and the nitrate warning (SARE: 'concentrates nitrate to toxic levels') are all confirmed. Edibility is genuinely uncontested.

audit_problems.name: Ostrich fern fiddleheads
problems: MATERIAL SAFETY GAP — lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina / A. angustum) is missing, and it is the one lookalike that defeats BOTH of the entry's stated field marks. The Alaska DNR Plant Materials Center fiddlehead profile states plainly that lady fern croziers 'also show a U-shaped groove down the inside of the stem, and for the inexperienced gatherer are hard to distinguish from the fiddleheads of Ostrich Fern,' and that 'both species of fiddleheads have brown papery scales.' Every tell in the entry's three lookalikes keys on absence of scales and/or absence of the groove — lady fern has both, so a forager following this entry has no rule that excludes it. Northern lady fern is native and common in rich moist woods across PA, the Northeast and the Midwest, i.e. exactly the listed regions and habitat. Not deadly (thiaminase, must be cooked), so this does not raise the caution tier, but the omission must be closed.

STRUCTURAL ID GAP — the deep U-shaped groove, which UMaine Bulletin #2540 gives as a primary recognition feature, is never stated as a positive requirement for the target species. It appears only as an absence in the lookalike tells. The 'parts' field asks the forager to confirm nothing but the papery brown scale, which alone does not distinguish ostrich fern from lady fern. Fixed by requiring both marks explicitly on every fiddlehead picked.

Cinnamon/interrupted fern is tagged danger 'unpalatable' while its own tell says 'Reported to cause illness' — internally contradictory, and the illness claim is unsourced and vague. The real, citable point is stronger: the Alaska DNR profile records speculation that the fiddleheads behind the 1994 poisoning cases 'may have actually been from Cinnamon Fern or Interrupted Fern (Osmunda species).' Retagged 'toxic' and the tell rewritten to state that attribution honestly as suspicion rather than fact.

Sensitive fern tell says 'no groove' in absolute terms. Sources phrase it as lacking the deep celery-like groove, not as being perfectly ungrooved. The absolute wording is the wrong failure direction: a forager who finds any shallow channel on a sensitive fern could conclude it must be ostrich fern. Sharpened to 'no deep celery-like channel' and added the corroborated thin, red-tinged-at-base stem detail.
Citation imprecision in the MMWR reference: the article is MMWR 43(37):677, 683-684 (23 Sept 1994), not a contiguous '677-684'. Corrected. The URL, title and date are genuine.

'No illness was linked to fiddleheads boiled or steamed 10+ minutes' is an absolute negative that the sources do not support in that form. UMaine and CDC say thorough cooking is what prevents the illness. Reworded to match. Also added 'discard the cooking water,' which the entry's cook-then-sauté instruction implies but never says.

Minor: 'a four-year UMaine study found repeat stripping drives crowns into decline' slightly misstates the finding — UMaine reports that crowns stripped of all fiddleheads annually declined and died WITHIN four years, while half-harvesting stayed productive. Rephrased. The underlying research is real (Dykeman, B.W. 1985, Effects of Crozier Removal on Growth of the Ostrich Fern, Can. J. Plant Sci. 65:1019-1023), now cited.

CHECKED AND CORRECT, no change needed: all four cited sources are real, authoritative and quoted accurately — UMaine Bulletin #2540 and #4198 ('Facts on Fiddleheads') match the entry nearly verbatim on the 2-6 inch size, the 'at least four fiddleheads' crown rule, the half-harvest with no follow-up flush, the 15-minute boil / 10-12 minute steam, and the sauté/stir-fry/microwave exclusion. Nothing fabricated.

CHECKED AND CORRECT: months [3,4] = April/May are right (UMaine: late April in southern Maine to mid/late May in far northern Maine; earlier at the PA southern edge). Regions are right and notably well-drawn — PA forms the southern border of the range and it extends west to South Dakota, while it reaches the west coast only in southern Alaska and British Columbia, so excluding 'northwest' is correct rather than an oversight.

CHECKED AND CORRECT: caution 'care' is the honest tier and was deliberately left unchanged. No lookalike here is acutely deadly to humans — bracken is a carcinogen (ptaquiloside, IARC 2B), sensitive fern is a thiaminase livestock toxin, Osmunda spp. are suspect, lady fern is mildly toxic raw. Under the stated rubric ('expert' only when a DEADLY lookalike exists), raising this to expert would be miscalibration. Edibility of properly cooked ostrich fern is genuinely uncontested — it is a commercial crop with extension-published cooking guidance.

audit_problems.name: Stinging nettle
problems: SCHEMA BREAK: the required `terrain: Terrain[]` field is missing entirely (src/data/foraging.ts:65). The object will not typecheck, and forageByTerrain() calls s.terrain.includes(...) at line 108 — it would throw at runtime. Added terrain: ['wetland','edge','disturbed'].

CAUTION SET TOO LOW — the headline defect. White snakeroot is a genuinely deadly lookalike: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox rates Ageratina altissima poison severity HIGH, all parts toxic, symptoms 'weakness, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, delirium, cardiac damage, prostration and eventually, coma.' The entry's own tell says 'can be fatal', yet danger is 'toxic' and caution is 'care'. Per the repo's own definitions (Caution 'expert' = 'a deadly lookalike exists', Lookalike danger 'deadly' exists as an enum value) this must be caution: 'expert' and danger: 'deadly'. As written the entry contradicts itself and under-warns.

THE SNAKEROOT FLOWER TELL IS USELESS IN SEASON. The tell leans on 'bright fuzzy white in flat clusters, not the greenish drooping tassels of nettle' — but white snakeroot blooms August–October (University of Illinois Extension HortAnswers; NC State: 'late summer to fall'), and nettle is picked as a pre-flowering shoot in Mar–Jun. During the entire harvest window neither plant has flowers. The tell had to be rebuilt around vegetative characters.

THE PETIOLE TELL IS FACTUALLY WRONG. 'the leaves sit on long 1–2 inch stalks' is offered as a snakeroot discriminator, but Urtica dioica petioles are 2.5–4 cm (1–1.6 in) and snakeroot petioles run 0.5–2.5 in — they overlap almost completely. A picker applying this tell can talk themselves into the wrong plant. Removed and replaced with an explicit warning not to use stalk length.

THE STING TEST IS DEFEATED BY THE ENTRY'S OWN INSTRUCTIONS. The only decisive tell given ('brush it bare-handed... nettle raises welts within seconds') is destroyed by 'Wear rubber gloves and long sleeves' in the parts field. Nothing tells the reader to do the bare-skin check BEFORE gloving up. Sequenced explicitly in the fix.

MISSING NON-CONTACT TELLS. Nothing in the entry lets you separate nettle from snakeroot by looking. Added two verified ones: nettle's stem is 4-angled/square and bristling with stinging hairs and it carries a pair of narrow stipules 5–15 mm at every leaf node (Go Botany, Native Plant Trust); snakeroot is an aster with a round, green, hairless stem and no stipules at all (Minnesota Wildflowers; NC State).

'if it doesn't sting, it isn't nettle' is a dangerously one-way heuristic as printed. It is true, but a reader can invert it into 'stingless = the harmless clearweed I just read about' — and white snakeroot is also stingless. Added the converse warning in the clearweed tell.

MONTHS MISS THE START OF THE SEASON for two of the four listed regions. months [3,4,5] = April–June, but in the maritime Northwest and coastal West nettle shoots are harvested from late February/early March, and March is peak in much of the mid-Atlantic/PA. Changed to [2,3,4,5] and added a regional-timing sentence to harvest.

No deadly lookalike is actually missing — this was checked hard. Candidates considered and rejected: water hemlock (Cicuta maculata) shares the streambank habitat exactly but has pinnately compound leaves on hollow, purple-streaked stems, not a visual confusable for a nettle top; hemp dogbane (Apocynum cannabinum) has opposite but entire, untoothed leaves and milky sap; dead-nettles/hemp nettle/motherwort are mints and harmless-to-mild. White snakeroot is the one real deadly confusable and it was present, just mis-rated.

SOURCES ARE ALL REAL — none fabricated. Verified live: NC State Urtica dioica, NC State Ageratina altissima, MDC wood nettle field guide, U. Missouri IPM MEG 2013 'Spring Wildcrafting: Going for the Greens' (also archived at ipm.missouri.edu/MEG/archive/2013/v19n3.pdf). OSU EM 9373 'Wild Edibles: Stinging Nettle' 403s to a fetcher but is confirmed genuine (catalog page plus PDF at extension.oregonstate.edu/sites/extd8/files/catalog/auto/EM9373.pdf, and an OSU impact story about the publication). Added three sources that carry the new tells.

MINOR, left as-is: regions omit southeast and southwest, although Urtica dioica ssp. gracilis does occur in the southern Appalachians (NC State says all three NC regions) and in western/southwestern mountains. The omission is conservative and creates no safety risk, so it was not changed.

Everything else checks out: edibility is genuinely uncontested (nettle and wood nettle are both mainstream extension-endorsed potherbs, MDC explicitly endorses cooked wood nettle); wood nettle's alternate-vs-opposite distinction is correct (MDC); cooking destroying the sting, the post-flowering cystolith caution, the tremetone toxin, horse nettle's solanine and yellow berries, and the red admiral / question mark / comma larval-host note are all accurate.

audit_problems.name: Dandelion
problems: BLOCKING BUG: regions: ["all"] is not a valid region id. The real model in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/seasonal-regional.ts (lines 9-19) is northeast, southeast, midwest, southcentral, mountain, west, and the filter at line 146 is `p.regions.includes(region)` — so "all" matches nothing and the entry would never render for any user. Also note the region ids in the task brief (southwest, northwest) do not exist in the codebase; the actual ids are southcentral and mountain. Fixed by enumerating the six real ids.

MISSING TOXIC LOOKALIKE — coltsfoot (Tussilago farfara). This is the most important gap: the entry explicitly recommends harvesting yellow flower heads for fritters and jelly in March-May, and coltsfoot is the classic early-spring dandelion-flower confusion on exactly the disturbed roadside/ditch/gravel ground the entry describes, common in the Northeast (incl. PA) and Midwest. It contains hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Ohio State Extension publishes an article literally titled 'Coltsfoot, Not Dandelion' (bygl.osu.edu/node/689). Added with a concrete tell: it flowers on bare ground with no leaves anywhere on the plant (leaves come weeks later), on a grey-woolly stalk clad in overlapping scale-like bracts, versus dandelion's smooth naked hollow scape rising from a leafy rosette.

MISSING TOXIC LOOKALIKE — butterweed / cressleaf groundsel (Packera glabella). A pyrrolizidine-alkaloid plant that blankets Midwest and Southeast fields yellow in April and overwinters as a ragged, deeply lobed basal rosette that sits squarely in the March-April greens window the entry recommends. OSU BYGL documents the PA content and the resulting liver disease (seneciosis). Added with tells: hollow ribbed purple-streaked stem with leaves running up it, many heads in a flat-topped cluster, and clear (not milky) sap.

The common groundsel tell only works on a bolted plant. Every mark listed (branched leafy upright stem, clusters of heads, black-tipped bracts) requires a flowering plant, but the entry sends the forager out for greens in March-April, when groundsel is still a small rosette of deeply lobed leaves that genuinely reads as a young dandelion. Rewrote to lead with the test that actually works at rosette stage: dandelion bleeds white latex from any break, groundsel's sap is clear and watery.

'cumulative, irreversible liver damage' overstates the cited source. UC IPM's actual wording is that pyrrolizidine alkaloids are toxic 'when ingested in large quantity, or even in small amounts over several weeks or months.' Reworded to keep the (correct and important) cumulative framing without the absolute claim.

The hairy cat's ear tell omits the strongest and most reliable field mark: dandelion's flower stalk is hollow and collapses when pinched, while cat's ear's is solid and wiry and carries small scale-like bracts. Both the cited MSU Extension post and NC State lead with the solid-vs-hollow / branched-vs-unbranched distinction, which is more dependable than leaf hairiness on a young plant. Added.

The sow thistle tell doesn't warn that Sonchus also bleeds milky sap — a forager who has just been told latex is the dandelion test could be misled into confirming a sow thistle. Added an explicit note that latex will not separate these two and the stem is the distinguishing feature.

months [2,3,4,9,10] (Mar-May, Oct-Nov) is too narrow now that regions cover the Southeast, South Central and West, where the entry's own advice ('best before the first flower buds open') falls in February. Added month 1.

The entry says every broken part bleeds white latex but never mentions that the latex can irritate skin. NC State's Plant Toolbox classes dandelion as a 'low severity poison' precisely for contact dermatitis from taraxinic acid in the sap. Added a clause.

VERIFIED CLEAN (no change needed): all five original sources are real and authoritative — I fetched NC State TurfFiles 'Common Dandelion', the NC State Plant Toolbox entry, the UC IPM common groundsel page, and the MU IPM article (David Trinklein, 'Spring Wildcrafting: Going for the Green(s)', Missouri Environment & Garden Newsletter, 5 March 2013), and resolved the MSU Extension January 2020 weed post on hairy cat's ear. No fabricated citations.

VERIFIED CLEAN (no change needed): caution 'care' is honest and correctly set. I searched specifically for a deadly confusable and there is none — NC State's own similar-species list (Arnica, Cichorium, Hypochaeris, Krigia, Pilosella, Senecio, Sonchus, Youngia, Erechtites) contains no lethal plant. The confusables are pyrrolizidine-alkaloid hepatotoxics whose danger is cumulative rather than acute, which is 'care', not 'expert'. Edibility is genuinely uncontested, and the herbicide/roadside contamination warning is well-founded and matches the MU source.

audit_problems.name: Garlic mustard
problems: MISSING DEADLY HAZARD — poison hemlock (Conium maculatum). The entry tells you to harvest 'second-year young tops, flower buds and white flowers' and to pull plants in bulk by the root in PA floodplains, and never mentions hemlock. Penn State Extension (extension.psu.edu/poison-hemlock-identification) puts poison hemlock in exactly that ground: a biennial that 'commonly grows along roadsides, at field edges, and in low-lying areas, near creeks and streams' throughout PA, standing 3-6 ft with white flowers in year two, with all parts poisonous and skin-contact risk requiring gloves. Olmsted Parks Conservancy documents garlic mustard and poison hemlock being pulled in the same sessions because 'their similar growth pattern leads us to attack them at the same time of year.' It is not a leaf-for-leaf twin (hemlock leaves are 3-4x pinnately compound and lacy), so I have written the tell to say so honestly — but its total absence from an entry whose harvest advice is 'take as much of as you can carry' is the single biggest gap.

MISSING TOXIC LOOKALIKE — kidneyleaf buttercup (Ranunculus abortivus), and it is a closer vegetative match to a garlic mustard rosette than lesser celandine is. UMass Amherst Weed Herbarium describes its basal leaves as 'round to heart or kidney-shaped with scalloped margins on long petioles'; it is native, grows in moist bottomland woods, lawns, trail edges and disturbed ground across the entry's whole range, and is toxic via protoanemonin (mouth/gut burning, skin blistering). Critically, the entry's own discriminator against lesser celandine — 'distinctly scallop-toothed' — does NOT separate garlic mustard from R. abortivus, so the published tell would actively mislead. Added with smell as the operative tell.

CAUTION SET TOO LOW. The file's own scale in src/data/foraging.ts defines 'expert' as 'a deadly lookalike exists'. With poison hemlock co-occurring in the same habitat, season and growth form as the plant part the entry recommends picking, 'care' understates it. Raised to 'expert'. Flagging this as a judgment call: if the maintainer decides a co-occurring deadly plant with obviously different leaves does not meet the bar for 'expert', the hemlock lookalike must still stay in the list.

OVER-RELIANCE ON THE GARLIC SMELL, with no caveat that it fades. Both toxic-lookalike tells in the original hinge entirely on smell, but Michigan State University Extension notes the odor is strongest in young spring tissue and 'less obvious with increasing age' — second-year and post-flowering plants can smell of little. A negative smell test is therefore not proof of a non-garlic-mustard later in the season. Caveat added to parts.

'TRACE CYANIDE' CONTRADICTS THE PAPER IT CITES. Cipollini & Gruner 2007 (J Chem Ecol 33(1):85-94) report cyanide reaching 100 ppm fresh weight — explicitly 'a level considered toxic to many vertebrates' — and highest in the young leaves of first-year plants, which is precisely the tissue the entry recommends as 'best flavour'. Calling that 'trace' downplays the entry's own source. Corrected to the actual figure and tied to the first-year rosette it recommends.

SCHEMA VIOLATION — the required 'terrain' field is missing. ForageSpecies in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts requires 'terrain: Terrain[]', and forageByTerrain() reads s.terrain. As submitted this object does not type-check and the species would never render in the terrain grouping. Added ['woodland','edge','wetland','disturbed'].

CUTLEAF TOOTHWORT IS INTERNALLY CONTRADICTORY — labelled danger:'unpalatable' while its own tell says 'Edible and pleasant'. The Lookalike danger enum is only 'deadly' | 'toxic' | 'unpalatable', so there is no honest value for a harmless native, and shipping an 'unpalatable' badge on a plant the text calls pleasant is a false statement to the reader. Moved the (genuinely useful, PSU-named) compound-vs-simple-leaf discriminator into 'harvest', where the don't-pull-natives conservation point already lives, and dropped it from lookalikes.

SEED COUNT OVERSTATED against both cited sources. 'Several thousand seeds per plant' is contradicted by Penn State Extension's own 'Ubiquitous Invasive Weed' page ('on average, 22 siliques, each with as many as 28 seeds', ~800 seeds total) and by MN DNR ('hundreds to thousands'). Corrected to 'hundreds to thousands'.

MINOR SOURCING GAP — the PSU lesser celandine page cited for it does not address toxicity, and nothing in the original list backs the 'Pennsylvania-listed noxious weed' claim. The claim itself is CORRECT (Ficaria verna is a PA Class B noxious weed), so I added the PA Department of Agriculture Controlled Plant & Noxious Weed Lists as the supporting citation rather than removing the claim.

VERIFIED SOUND, no changes needed: all seven original sources are real and reachable — nothing fabricated, including Cipollini & Gruner 2007 (DOI 10.1007/s10886-006-9205-x). The lesser celandine tell checks out verbatim against PSU ('glossy and kidney-shaped', 'mostly smooth edges with some gentle lobes or slightly scalloped appearance', tubers 'like tiny potatoes', bulblets on stems, floodplains). The ground ivy tell checks out against NC State (4-angled/square stems, kidney-shaped toothed leaves, blue-violet flowers, aromatic, 'Toxic to horses'). Bagging pulled plants because flowering plants set seed after pulling is confirmed by MN DNR. Months [2,3,4,5] are plausible (PSU: flowers late April through June). Regions are supported — Oregon ODA rates it B/T, first documented 1959, so 'northwest' is right; omitting 'west' is defensible since the only California records are isolated 2020/2022 streamside detections. Edibility is genuinely uncontested; garlic mustard is a widely eaten pot-herb and the only real caveat is dose (cyanide + glucosinolates), which the corrected text now states accurately. During research I also hit spice.alibaba.com pages claiming a '73% of misidentification attempts occur before May' statistic for garlic mustard — that is SEO content-farm output with no traceable study behind it. audit_problems.name: Ramps (wild leeks)
problems: SAFETY (worst defect) — the false-hellebore tell uses habitat as a disqualifier and is wrong for two thirds of the listed range. The entry says false hellebore 'favours seeps, swamps and floodplains'. That is true of Veratrum viride, but the southern-Appalachian species implicated in ramp-confusion poisonings is V. parviflorum, which grows in rich deciduous forest at 800–2,030 m in AL, GA, KY, NC, SC, TN, VA and WV — i.e. the exact upland ramp habitat the entry describes; V. woodii occupies rich upland woods in the Midwest. A forager on a dry rich slope in Georgia or Missouri could use the entry's habitat cue to rule out the deadly plant. Source: Seale & McDougal, Molecules 2022;27(16):5349 (PMC9412450) — 'V. parviflorum growth season coincides with wild ramps (Allium tricoccum); furthermore, it has led to the accidental ingestion of V. parviflorum, resulting in cardiac and gastrointestinal toxicity'; Emory Dept. of Emergency Medicine ramps advisory names both V. parviflorum and V. viride.

MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE — fly poison (Amianthium muscitoxicum). Native NY to FL and west to MO/OK, in moist woods and oak forest, so it overlaps the northeast/southeast/midwest range given. All parts carry neurotoxic alkaloids, concentrated in an onion-like bulb; NC State Extension states ingestion can be fatal. Grass/strap-like leaves make leaf confusion less likely than Veratrum, but the bulb is the classic trap for anyone digging. Added to the corrected entry.

MISSING PRACTICAL SAFETY STEP — the smell test is stated as absolute with no protocol. Once you have crushed a few ramps, your hands, knife and bag all smell of onion, so a hellebore leaf mixed into the bunch will smell of onion too. The entry never says to tear and sniff each individual plant before it goes in the bag. This is the actual real-world failure mode behind the Vermont and Georgia poisoning clusters.

OVERSTATED CLAIM — 'Fatal poisonings are on record from leaves gathered alongside wild alliums' (lily-of-the-valley). Severe, hospitalised Convallaria poisonings from wild-garlic confusion are documented in Europe, but human fatalities are rare-to-generally-unreported; the deaths in the European wild-garlic literature are overwhelmingly Colchicum autumnale, not Convallaria. NC State's own toolbox (cited by the entry) rates Convallaria severity as low / 'toxic only if large quantities eaten'. Keeping danger:deadly is fine as a conservative call, but the fatality sentence as written is not verifiable. Softened.

WEAK/UNRELIABLE TELL — 'no red-purple base' is used as a lily-of-the-valley disqualifier. The red-purple sheath is a good positive sign for A. tricoccum but is variable, and the narrow-leaved ramp (A. tricoccum var. burdickii / A. burdickii) has pale whitish bases. A better, dig-based tell for Convallaria is the creeping horizontal rhizome with roots along its length and no distinct onion-like bulb. Corrected.

SUSTAINABILITY RULE MISSTATES ITS OWN SOURCE — 'take no more than one plant in ten from a large patch' drops the frequency. Rock, Beckage & Gross (2004) support 10% of a population once per decade, not 10% per visit or per year; Quebec's assessment is that an annual take of 5–15% of bulbs is enough to drive a colony into decline. As written the rule reads as a licence for repeat annual 10% harvests. Corrected.

LEAF-ONLY HARVEST OVERSOLD — 'gives you nearly all the flavour at a fraction of the ecological cost' implies leaf harvest is near-free. Dion, Bussières & Lapointe (Agroforestry Systems 2016;90(6):979–995) note leaf-limited harvest can still slow growth by drawing down carbon and nutrient reserves depending on timing and intensity. Softened to 'lower impact, not free'.

MONTHS TOO NARROW — [3,4] (Apr–May) misses March. Penn State Extension gives leaves March–May; Illinois Extension has ramps emerging in central Illinois in late March; Nilson et al. give emergence/senescence spanning roughly March 1 to May 30. With southeast and midwest listed, March belongs in the range. Changed to [2,3,4].

MINOR BOTANY — 'Two broad flat leaves' is stated as definitional. Ramps carry one, two or three leaves; Nilson et al. (2022) found three-leaved plants significantly heavier and recommend targeting them, which matters for the harvest advice. Corrected.

ATTRIBUTION — the 250%/400% weight figures are credited vaguely to 'Penn State's work' and the cited Extension factsheet does not contain them. They come from Nilson SE, Burkhart EP, Jordan RT, Lambert JD, Agroforestry Systems 2023;97(1):97–107, doi:10.1007/s10457-022-00790-3 (covered by the cited PSU News piece). Primary citation added. The 'fewer ramps per pound is more ramps in the ground' quote is real — it is Sarah Nilson in that PSU News release.

GOOD NEWS — no fabricated citations. All six original URLs return HTTP 200 and say what the entry claims; Rock/Beckage/Gross 2004 verified via Crossref as Biological Conservation 116(2):227–234, doi:10.1016/S0006-3207(03)00193-9. The habitat text (east/north-facing slopes, seeps, calcium-rich slightly acidic soil over limestone, sugar maple/blue cohosh associates) is taken accurately from the Penn State Extension factsheet. Edibility is uncontested, regions are correct (A. tricoccum does not occur in west/southwest/northwest), and caution:expert is the right level.

audit_problems.name: Common blue violet
problems: BROKEN SOURCE URL (real article, wrong path): the UMN Extension citation is given as https://extension.umn.edu/news/wild-edibles-common-blue-violets, which 403s/does not resolve. The article is genuine but lives at https://extension.umn.edu/natural-resources-news/wild-edibles-common-blue-violets. Fixed.

MISSING TOXIC LOOKALIKE - WILD GINGER (Asarum canadense, plus southeastern Hexastylis/heartleaf): heart-shaped leaves, low groundcover, blooming mid-spring, in exactly the 'moist woodland floors and stream banks' habitat this entry names. NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox gives it a poison rating for leaves, roots and stems and states plainly 'Do not consume any part of this plant' because aristolochic acid is nephrotoxic and a carcinogen. Foraging literature routinely names it as the violet-leaf confusable in woodland settings. This was the single largest gap and it has been added with a concrete tell (paired leaves on a short stem, 3-6 in, leathery, dull gray-green, hairy, strong ginger smell when crushed vs. violet's smaller, matte, individually stalked leaves rising separately from a basal crown with no smell).

UNCITED TOXICITY CLAIM: the yellow-violet 'strongly laxative' assertion had no supporting source in the list, and 'strongly' overstates what the literature says. NC State's Viola pubescens page says flowers are 'edible in limited quantities as they can have a laxative effect.' Wording softened to match the source and the NC State page added as a citation.

MISSING OPERATIVE SAFETY RULE: the entry recommends young leaves raw in salad but never states the one rule its own cited UMN Extension source leads with - that the leaves are the confusable part, so beginners should take flowers only, and leaves only from a plant they have actually seen in flower. Every confusion in this entry (celandine, wild ginger, marsh marigold) happens pre-bloom, so this omission mattered. Added to harvest.
