MONTHS TOO NARROW FOR THE STATED REGIONS: months were [2,3,4,5] (Mar-Jun) while regions include southeast, where NC State documents Viola sororia blooming from February. Changed to [1,2,3,4,5].

MARSH MARIGOLD LEAF SIZE UNDERSTATED: entry said 'up to 4 inches across'; NC State gives 3-6 inches, enlarging further after flowering, and other sources go higher. Since sheer size is a main discriminator from a violet leaf, the understatement blunted the tell. Corrected to 3-6 inches and larger after bloom, and 'not eaten raw' strengthened to match NC State's 'no part of this plant should ever be eaten raw.'

MISLEADING HABITAT FRAMING: 'shares with lesser celandine and garlic mustard, which is precisely the problem' lumps garlic mustard (edible, harmless, a common co-occurring rosette) in with the actually toxic lesser celandine. Reworded so the hazard points only where it belongs.

FABRICATED-CITATION CHECK - all six original sources verified as real, none invented: NC State Viola sororia (confirms edible leaves/flowers, heart-shaped scalloped leaves to 4 in, Feb-May bloom in NC, 38 states); Penn State Extension 'Don't Be Deceived by This Beguiling Springtime Plant' (confirms the celandine tell almost verbatim - 'glossy and kidney-shaped, mostly smooth edges', 'bright yellow with 8 or more narrow petals', tubers and above-ground bulblets, and the marsh marigold comparison); UMD Extension Lesser Celandine (confirms kidney-shaped waxy leaves, tuberous roots, axillary bulblets); PA DCNR Invasive Plant Fact Sheets (page exists, lesser celandine sheet present under the older name Ranunculus ficaria); Illinois Extension 'Embracing the common blue violet' by Christopher Enroth, 2017-06-07 (confirms roots not edible, fritillary larval host, African violet warning). Only the UMN path was wrong. Separately, I checked and REJECTED an FDA Import Alert URL for aristolochic acid that appeared in search results (accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_141.html) - it 404s, so it is not cited; the aristolochic acid claim rests on NC State instead.

CAUTION LEVEL AUDITED AND UPHELD AT 'care' (not raised to expert): I specifically hunted for an acutely deadly confusable and found none. The realistic confusables are lesser celandine (protoanemonin - GI irritation, dermatitis), marsh marigold (protoanemonin, NC State 'low severity poison'), wild ginger (serious but chronic - kidney damage and urinary-tract carcinogenicity, not acute death), and yellow violets (laxative). No death-camas/lily-of-the-valley-class hazard exists here, and the flower is unmistakable. 'care' is the honest setting; raising it to 'expert' would be inflation.

EDIBILITY IS UNCONTESTED: leaves and flowers of Viola sororia are agreed edible across university extension sources; roots/rhizomes emetic, correctly excluded by the original entry. No literature split. Species is appropriate to publish.

audit_problems.name: Wild garlic (field garlic)
problems: CAUTION SET TOO LOW (safety-critical). The entry rates the whole species `care`, and rates Star-of-Bethlehem merely `toxic` with the consequence described as 'gastric poisoning'. That is wrong on the mechanism. Ornithogalum umbellatum is a CARDIAC GLYCOSIDE plant: Cornell's Plants Poisonous to Livestock database names its poisons as convallatoxin and convalloside (the same cardenolide as lily-of-the-valley), and Purdue's toxic plant guide names glycoside rhodexin A / rhodexoside and groups it with foxglove and oleander. Ingestion can be fatal, not merely emetic. It shares the exact habitat the entry describes (lawns, PA), it is present and pre-flowering during the entire Mar-May harvest window given, and its bulb looks like a small onion. Under the project's own rule ('expert if a DEADLY lookalike exists'), caution must be `expert` and this lookalike's danger must be `deadly`. Citation mismatch too: the cardiac-glycoside claim is footnoted to the NC State toolbox page, which actually says toxic principle = saponin, severity = medium, symptoms = gastric. The cited source does not support the claim made.

MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE #1: DEATH CAMAS. This is the single biggest gap. The entry claims the `midwest` region, and Toxicoscordion nuttallii (Nuttall's death camas) runs from central Kansas and Oklahoma east through southern Missouri, Arkansas and Louisiana. It is the archetypal fatal wild-onion foraging error in the United States: a 2024 case report in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine (PMID 39472268) documents SEVEN family members acutely poisoned by Toxicoscordion venenosum after foraging for wild onions. Its bulb is onion-like, its toxins (zygacine/zygadenine) are sodium-channel activators causing vomiting, bradycardia, collapsing blood pressure and death. An entry about foraging Allium in the midwest that omits death camas is not publishable.

MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE #2: FLY POISON (Amianthium muscitoxicum). Native from New York and Pennsylvania south to Florida and west to Missouri and Oklahoma, i.e. squarely inside all three claimed regions, and present in the Flora of Pennsylvania. Onion-like bulb, grass-like basal leaves from that bulb, alkaloid neurotoxins concentrated in the bulb, all parts poisonous. It is also confusingly nicknamed 'crow poison', the same folk name used for Nothoscordum, which compounds the risk for a reader searching the name.

THE SMELL TEST IS STATED AS INFALLIBLE WITH ITS ONE KNOWN FAILURE MODE OMITTED. The harvest text calls the crush-and-sniff rule 'absolute, non-negotiable'. The rule is sound in principle but the entry omits the caveat that makes it fail in practice: once you have crushed one Allium, the odor clings to your fingers and the next plant you crush will also smell of onion. Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) flags exactly this as the pitfall of the smell test in its wild-garlic doppelganger work. The entry, as written, walks a reader through a patch crushing leaf after leaf with contaminated hands and tells them the resulting sniff is definitive. Must add: sniff each plant with clean hands or a freshly torn leaf, and if in any doubt wash first and re-test.

MISSING COMMON NON-DEADLY CONFUSABLE: false garlic / crow poison (Nothoscordum bivalve), an extremely common southeast and midwest lawn plant that looks like a small wild onion with six-tepaled white flowers but has NO onion or garlic odour when crushed. Its toxicity is poorly characterised (which is itself a reason not to eat it). It is the plant most likely to make a reader in the claimed regions actually exercise the smell test, so it belongs in the list.

INTERNAL MONTH CONTRADICTION. months = [2,3,4,9,10] = Mar, Apr, May, Oct, Nov. But the `parts` text tells the reader to harvest aerial bulbils that form 'in June' (month 5, absent), and the `habitat` text sells the plant as bright green tufts on 'a brown late-winter lawn' (Feb, month 1, absent). Field garlic is a winter perennial that emerges in autumn and stays green through winter, so the prose is right and the array is wrong. Corrected to [1,2,3,4,5,9,10].

MISLABELLED LOOKALIKE: Allium canadense is given danger `unpalatable` while its own tell says 'Not dangerous - a native edible Allium'. A choice native edible is filed under a danger category. The flat/solid vs round/hollow contrast is genuinely useful and worth keeping (SARE and Penn State Extension both draw it), but it must be labelled honestly rather than occupying a danger slot.

REGIONS ARE INCOMPLETE, AND THE FIX IS NOT FREE. Allium vineale is naturalised well beyond the three listed regions - established west of the Cascade crest from southwestern British Columbia to California. Adding `northwest`/`west` would be more accurate, BUT it would drag in western death camas (Toxicoscordion venenosum), the deadliest Allium confusable in North America and the subject of the 2024 seven-person poisoning. I have left the regions conservative at northeast/southeast/midwest rather than expand coverage into a region whose worst hazard the entry does not yet handle; flagging it so the decision is deliberate.

MINOR: the entry treats field garlic itself as wholly benign. NC State notes low-level toxicity in humans from the sulfides (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea if eaten in quantity), which is worth one clause given the entry tells readers it is 'considerably stronger' than scallions and encourages free harvesting.

SOURCES CHECKED - NONE FABRICATED, ONE STALE, ONE MISCITED. Verified live and on-topic: NC State toolbox Allium vineale (confirms hollow round leaves, aerial bulbils in a sack-like membrane, fall emergence, edible); Virginia Tech weedid profile/650 (real, returns 403 to automated fetches but is indexed with the correct title); Clemson HGIC weed-of-the-month-wild-garlic (real, confirms hollow round vs flat leaves and offset bulblets); SARE Manage Weeds on Your Farm (real, and is the source confirming A. canadense leaves are flat and solid); NC State Ornithogalum umbellatum (real, but see the miscitation above). The CSU link is REAL and correct in content - plant 116 is indeed Narcissus, with lycorine and phenanthridine alkaloids and cardiac arrhythmias in large ingestions - but the csuvth.colostate.edu URL is stale and 301-redirects; updated to the current poisonousplants.cvmbs.colostate.edu form. The entry's claim of 'published cases of families poisoned after mistaking the bulbs for onions' is TRUE and now cited directly (Ageta et al., Acute Medicine & Surgery 2020; 195 Japanese cases 2009-2019 including one death).

EDIBILITY ITSELF IS UNCONTESTED - this is the entry's strongest point and the reason the verdict is FIX rather than REMOVE. Allium vineale is unambiguously edible, non-native, weedy, and recommended for harvest by multiple extension services. The morphological tells given (round hollow leaves, white-striped flat Star-of-Bethlehem leaves, flat solid A. canadense leaves) all check out against Penn State, Virginia Tech, Clemson, NC State and SARE. The failures are of omission and of understated danger, not of species identity.

audit_problems.name: Morel
problems: VERPA TELL IS WRONG AS STATED (most substantive error). It says 'On yellow and black morels the cap is fused to the stem all the way down to its base.' Half-free morels (Morchella punctipes in the East, M. populiphila in the West) are TRUE morels in the black-morel clade whose cap is attached roughly halfway down and hangs free below. A forager applying the entry's cap-attachment rule to a half-free morel gets a false 'reject' - and worse, someone who has heard of half-free morels may use that as license to accept a Verpa. The decisive test for Verpa is the stem, not the cap: every true morel including the half-free is one hollow chamber; Verpa is stuffed with cotton-candy-like fibres. The entry mentions the stuffed stem but frames cap attachment as the primary rule. Fixed by naming half-free morels explicitly and demoting cap attachment below the slice test. (Sources: MSU Extension E2755; MushroomExpert.com Morchella punctipes / Verpa bohemica accounts.)

GYROMITRA TELL OMITS THE HABITAT AND TIMING OVERLAP - a real safety gap, because the entry's own habitat text sends Western foragers to burn sites. Gyromitra esculenta is abundant in montane conifer forest of the western US, favours disturbed and recently burned ground, and fruits at snowmelt in the same brief window as true morels. False morels appear inside recent burn perimeters alongside burn morels. The entry tells people where to go without telling them the deadly lookalike is fruiting in the same place at the same time. Added to the tell.

GYROMITRA LOOKALIKE NAMES ONLY TWO EASTERN SPECIES (G. esculenta, G. caroliniana) while the entry sets regions to 'all' and specifically directs people to Western conifer burns. The Western snow / bull-nose false morel (Gyromitra montana / G. gigas) is unnamed. Added, and the tell now points at the genus rather than a two-species list.

MONTHS ARE SHORT AT THE TOP END FOR THE WEST. [2,3,4,5] = Mar-Jun. With regions 'all' and an explicit Western burn-site habitat note, Rocky Mountain burn morels fruit June INTO July at roughly 8,000-11,000 ft, and natural black morels at 7,000-9,500 ft run into late June. Added month 6 (July). Month 1 (Feb) was considered for the Deep South and deliberately left out: late February is an occasional warm-year edge case, and the reliable Deep South start is the first half of March.

'HEAT-LABILE TOXINS' CLAIM WAS UNDER-CITED, though it turns out to be correct. True morels do contain small amounts of hydrazine-type toxins that are destroyed by thorough cooking (Lagrange & Vernoux, Toxins 2020, 12(8), 482). Note also that FDA found the Montana outbreak morels were imported CULTIVATED morels, which strengthens rather than weakens the point - correct species, correct sourcing, still two deaths from undercooking. Added the Toxins citation so the claim is verifiable.

MINOR, NOT FIXED: the harvest advice 'carry them in a mesh or basket bag so spores drop as you walk' is forager folklore with no supporting evidence (morels fruit from established mycelium; walk-and-drop reseeding is unsupported). It is harmless and widely repeated, so it was left in place, but it is not a verifiable claim in the way the rest of the entry now is.

MINOR: Helvella danger level 'toxic' and the hydrazine claim check out (Helvella species carry monomethylhydrazine-type compounds), but Helvella is a weak confusable compared with Gyromitra and Verpa - saddle-shaped flap, no pits at all. Kept, wording tightened.

audit_problems.name: Chicken of the Woods
problems: REGIONS ARE WRONG AND SELF-CONTRADICTORY (main defect). regions is ["all"], yet the entry's own lookalike tell says "In the West, true L. sulphureus does not occur at all." That claim is correct — MushroomExpert (Kuo) and the literature put L. sulphureus "east of the Rocky Mountains" — so listing all six regions puts the entry in season for west/northwest/southwest users for a mushroom that is not there. In the Northwest essentially every Laetiporus is L. conifericola on conifers, i.e. the species the entry tells you to leave. Corrected to northeast, southeast, midwest.

THE HOST-TREE TELL FAILS EXACTLY WHERE regions:["all"] SENDS PEOPLE. The tell says "look at the host tree, not the mushroom" and flags only conifers plus "L. gilbertsonii on eucalyptus" — implying hardwood/oak = safe. But L. gilbertsonii grows on oaks as well as eucalyptus in California, and the MSSF/NAMA toxicology record includes cases from oak-grown and conifer-grown material. A Californian reading this entry finds a bright orange bracket on a coast live oak, applies the entry's test, and eats the species with the documented poisoning record. Tell rewritten to say the hardwood test is not valid west of the Rockies.

YEW IS NOT NAMED. The conifer list is "pine, hemlock, spruce, fir, larch/tamarack" — no yew (Taxus). Yew is the one host with a genuinely serious concern (taxine alkaloids are cardiotoxic; the practical risk is needles and bark twigs embedded in the fruitbody's folds surviving cleaning), and suburban foragers do not mentally file a clipped yew hedge under "conifer." Added explicitly.

"LOCUST" IS LISTED AS A RECOMMENDED HOST. The habitat line advertises "cherry, beech and locust." The evidence here is genuinely split — Wikipedia lists black locust among normal hosts, but avoid-locust advice is near-universal in the foraging literature (usually bundled with yew/eucalyptus/conifer). By the entry set's own standard — prefer well-agreed, leave out what is contested — locust should not be sold as a prime host. Replaced with maple (UMass CAFE names maple and beech alongside oak) and a one-line caveat in parts.

OVERSTATED CAUSAL CLAIM. "the conifer- and eucalyptus-associated species cause vomiting and chills far more often than hardwood L. sulphureus" is stronger than the toxicology source supports. Duffy (Toxic Fungi of Western North America, MykoWeb) records that the eucalyptus-substrate thesis "was later in question as more cases produced by Laetiporus growing on oak and conifers were reported." Direction of the advice is safe; the certainty was hedged.
STALE SOURCE URL. The UMass link (ag.umass.edu/landscape/fact-sheets/...) 301-redirects to www.umass.edu/agriculture-food-environment/landscape/fact-sheets/.... Canonical URL substituted.

CHECKS THAT PASSED — no deadly lookalike is missing. I specifically hunted for one: jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus illudens) is severely GI-toxic but not deadly and is already listed with a correct, concrete tell (gilled and stalked with decurrent blade-like gills vs. a stalkless shelf with a pore surface). Conifer Laetiporus are covered. I considered and deliberately excluded Hapalopilus croceus (orange oak polypore) — it does resemble a young chicken, but it is rare, red-listed, and its toxicity literature is thin, so it fails the "well-known and widely agreed" bar. Phaeolus schweinitzii and Bondarzewia berkeleyi are covered by the conifer rule and by color respectively. Consequently caution "care" is honestly set, not too low — "expert" would require a deadly confusable and there is none.

CHECKS THAT PASSED — all five sources are real, correctly titled, correctly attributed, and say what the entry implies. Verified by fetching each: UF/IFAS PP358 exists with that exact title and contains the raw/undercooked GI warning and the allergy caveat; MDC's field guide page exists, gives season "May–November" (exactly months 4–10, so the months field is well supported) and the swollen-lips/small-first-portion advice the entry paraphrases; UMass CAFE confirms brown rot and oak/maple/beech hosts; the Cornell Mushroom Blog post "Eating the Chicken of the Woods" (Elan Margulies, 31 Oct 2006) exists and carries the conifer/L. huroniensis warning; Tom Volk's July 2001 fungus is indeed L. cincinnatus and confirms the white-pored rosette-from-soil-at-oak-base description. Nothing fabricated.

CHECKS THAT PASSED — edibility is not meaningfully contested for hardwood-grown eastern material, and the entry already handles the real residual risk (idiosyncratic reactions in a minority of eaters, cook thoroughly, small first portion). Months 4–10 are plausible and directly source-backed.

audit_problems.name: Hen of the Woods (Maitake)
problems: SCIENTIFIC NAME IS MISSPELLED (real error): the entry gives 'Sparassis spatulata'. The accepted binomial is Sparassis spathulata (synonym S. herbstii) — confirmed on MDC's own Eastern Cauliflower Mushroom page, iNaturalist taxon 334319, and MushroomExpert. A wrong binomial breaks verifiability, which is the one thing that must not break.

MISSING LOOKALIKE — dyer's polypore (Phaeolus schweinitzii): it fruits as a brown rosette/overlapping shelves at the base of a tree in exactly the same search image and season (early August–September in southern New England per UMass Extension), and it is inedible. Not deadly, so it does not change the caution level, but it is a genuine field confusion the entry omits. The tell is crisp and decisive: conifers ONLY (never oak), velvety yellowish/reddish-brown cap AND a brown pore surface — hen of the woods is on hardwood with a WHITE pore surface.

SOUTHEAST REGION IS OVERSTATED: Grifola frondosa is common in southern Appalachia but 'very unusual within 100 miles of the Gulf of Mexico and is not known from Florida.' Left unqualified this sends Gulf-coast and Florida users hunting a species that does not occur there — and the large pale rosette they WOULD find at an oak base in the Deep South is Bondarzewia berkeleyi, i.e. the lookalike. Region kept, habitat text qualified.

BERKELEY'S POLYPORE SIZE RANGE IS TOO NARROW: entry says '6–10 in.' caps; MDC gives 3–12 inches. A forager measuring a 4-inch cream fan could wrongly rule out Bondarzewia on size. Also 'flesh is woody-tough everywhere except the extreme growing edge' is true of mature specimens but not young ones — MDC describes young flesh as 'thick, firm' and cuttable, and edible.

SPARASSIS DANGER LABEL IS FACTUALLY WRONG: it is tagged danger 'unpalatable', but MDC calls the eastern cauliflower mushroom 'an excellent edible.' The real hazard is ID-confidence, not the mushroom. I left the enum value as 'unpalatable' because I could not verify the schema's allowed values — if the enum has an 'edible'/'none'/'harmless' option, use it here. The tell now carries the nuance explicitly.

MERIPILUS DANGER LABEL IS CONSERVATIVE (flagged, not changed): MDC calls the black-staining polypore 'a good edible, when young and fresh.' 'unpalatable' errs in the safe direction and multiple sources do report GI upset and mediocre flavor, so I kept it.

MISSING 'NEVER RAW' AND OWN-SPECIES REACTION NOTE: the entry said 'cook thoroughly' but never said not to eat it raw, and did not mention that correctly-identified maitake causes GI upset in a minority of people and that (rare) allergy exists. Added to parts.

HARVEST TEXT ASSERTS A FALSE MECHANISM: 'leave the butt attached to the tree — the same hen typically refruits for years' implies the leftover butt causes the refruiting. Refruiting comes from the mycelium already established in the roots and lower trunk (UMass: G. frondosa causes a white pocket rot of roots and lower trunk); picking the fruiting body does not harm it. Reworded so the sustainable advice stays but the reasoning is correct.

MONTHS WIDENED: [8,9,10] (Sep–Nov) matched MDC exactly, but UMass Extension says fruiting runs 'from late summer through the autumn season,' so August flushes are real. Added month 7 and noted the mid-September to early October peak — plus the fact that an August hen overlaps peak black-staining polypore and dyer's polypore season, which makes the lookalike check matter more early in the window.

VERIFIED SOUND — no change needed: (1) All five original sources are REAL and authoritative. I fetched every one: three MDC field-guide pages, the UMass CAFE Grifola root-and-butt-rot fact sheet, and the Illinois DNR Wild About Fungi page. Nothing fabricated. (2) NO DEADLY LOOKALIKE IS MISSING — Grifola frondosa genuinely has none; every confusable is another polypore or Sparassis, none lethal. (3) caution 'care' is therefore correctly calibrated per the stated rule, not too low. (4) The original three lookalikes match MDC's own lookalike list for this species exactly. (5) The tells check out: Meripilus blackening 'within minutes' is accurate; hen's pores are genuinely 'angular; white to yellowish' (MDC), so the pore-vs-ribbon-fold finger test is correct. (6) Edibility is uncontested — choice edible, commercially cultivated as maitake.

audit_problems.name: Giant Puffball
problems: SAFETY-CRITICAL, WRONG TELL: The Scleroderma lookalike says the flesh is 'marbled grey-purple to blackish-purple inside even when quite young'. This is contradicted by the entry's OWN cited source. Missouri Dept. of Conservation, Pigskin Puffball: 'When young, the inside is nearly white but soon becomes marbled, then purplish, then blackish with age.' A very young earthball cut open shows whitish flesh, so a forager applying this rule would get a false all-clear on a toxic mushroom. The dependable tells are the thick rind-like peridium, warty/scaly yellow-brown surface, small size (1-4 in), and firm rubbery texture - not interior colour alone.

BROKEN/INCORRECT SOURCE URL: 'https://herbarium.usu.edu/fun-with-fungi/giant-puffballs' does not exist - it 307-redirects to the herbarium homepage. The real Utah State Intermountain Herbarium page is at https://artsci.usu.edu/herbarium/activities_fun-stuff/fun-facts-about-fungi/giant-puffballs (verified: 'found in the central and eastern USA and Canada', season 'late Summer and Fall', 'cut it open... Do not eat anything with a brown, black, purple, or yellow interior').

WEAK / SELF-UNDERMINING SOURCE: The Iowa State Extension link is real but is a 2005 Yard and Garden lawn-nuisance article that uses the obsolete name 'Langermannia giganteum' and states puffballs 'pose no danger to people, pets, or plants'. That is not an authority for a foraging safety entry and contradicts the entry's own warnings. Replaced with the verified Penn State Extension (Pike County Master Gardener) giant puffball page, which is northeast-relevant and gives the cut-in-half test.

CITATION DOES NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM IT IS ATTACHED TO: The NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Amanita bisporigera is real, but describes only the mature mushroom (cap, ring, sac-like volva) and says nothing about the button/egg stage or confusion with puffballs. The egg-stage tell is actually supported by the NPS Species Spotlight page ('The button or egg-stage of poisonous gilled mushrooms mimic puffballs until vertically sliced into revealing the future stem and cap of the Amanita in cross-section'). NC State retained only as documentation that the species exists and is lethal.

MONTHS TOO BROAD AT THE FRONT END: months [4..9] = May-Oct. Only MDC's Missouri-specific 'May-October' supports May/June. Penn State says 'autumn', USU says 'late Summer and Fall', and the entry's own habitat text says 'a few days after a soaking late-summer rain'. Narrowed to [6,7,8,9] = Jul-Oct, with the early-flush caveat moved into the habitat text.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION 1: 'parts' says to peel off the 'tough outer skin', while the Scleroderma tell describes giant puffballs as 'thin-skinned'. Reworded to 'thin but tough' so the contrast with Scleroderma's thick rind stays meaningful.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION 2 / IMPRECISE TELL: The Amanita egg is described as wrapped in a 'leathery universal veil'. 'Leathery' is precisely the word that identifies Scleroderma's rind; the universal veil of A. bisporigera / A. phalloides is thin and membranous. Using the same adjective for both blurs the two most important tells in the entry.

SCOPE OF THE EGG-STAGE WARNING TOO NARROW: the lookalike is named only as Amanita. Any immature gilled mushroom still enclosed in its universal veil can look like a small white ball; the slice-everything rule should be framed that way rather than as an Amanita-only concern.
MINOR: 'S. bovista' is listed alongside S. citrinum but only S. citrinum is covered by the cited MDC page. Generalised the lookalike to Scleroderma spp. so the citation actually covers the claim.

NOT A DEFECT (checked and cleared): no deadly lookalike is missing - Amanita/gilled egg stage is the only lethal confusable and it is present; caution 'expert' is correctly set; edibility is uncontested (NPS lists puffballs among the 'Foolproof Four') with the known laxative/GI effect in some people already disclosed; regions northeast/midwest/southeast and the 'mainly east of the Rockies, western species is C. booniana' note are consistent with USU's 'central and eastern USA and Canada'.
